1. Functional Analysis  
   The function `DecodeChunk` is responsible for reading and decoding a single “chunk” (either a tile or a scanline block) from an in-memory EXR image buffer.  Here is the high-level flow:  
   • Initialization  
     – Read header parameters: number of channels, compression type, data window (width/height), tile size if tiled, etc.  
     – Compute how many scanlines belong to each block when using scanline compression (ZIP, PIZ, ZFP have their own block‐sizes).  
     – Call `ComputeChannelLayout` to figure out per‐channel byte offsets in the final pixel buffer and total pixel data size.  
   • Tiled Format Path (`exr_header->tiled == true`)  
     – Allocate an array of `EXRTile` structs, one per tile.  
     – For each tile index:  
       • Allocate a tile‐sized image buffer for all channels.  
       • Read the 4 tile coordinates (x, y, level_x, level_y) from the data stream and byte‐swap them to host endianness.  
       • Read the 32‐bit data‐length `data_len` and byte‐swap it.  
       • Advance the pointer past the coordinate + length fields.  
       • Call `DecodeTiledPixelData(...)` to decompress/decode the tile’s pixel data into the allocated buffer.  
       • Store the tile’s offsets and levels in the `EXRTile` struct.  
       • Record the total number of tiles in `exr_image->num_tiles`.  
   • Scanline Format Path (`exr_header->tiled == false`)  
     – Allocate one big image buffer for the entire frame.  
     – In parallel over each scanline‐block index `y`:  
       • Check that reading 8 bytes (scanline number + data length) doesn’t run past buffer end.  
       • Read and byte‐swap the scanline index (`line_no`) and block data length (`data_len`).  
       • Compute how many actual scanlines this block covers (`num_lines`).  
       • Adjust `line_no` by subtracting the window’s minimum Y.  
       • Advance the data pointer past the 8‐byte header.  
       • Call `DecodePixelData(...)` to decode or decompress those scanlines into the big image buffer at the correct offset.  
       • If any of the above checks/decode calls fail, mark `invalid_data = true`.  
   • Finalization  
     – If any out‐of‐bounds or decode‐failure was detected (`invalid_data`), return an error.  
     – Overwrite the header’s pixel‐type array with the requested types (indicating that decoding produced those types).  
     – Fill out `exr_image->num_channels`, `width`, and `height`, then return success.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   • Out-of-bounds reads  
     – Before reading tile headers, the code checks `offset + header_bytes <= size`  
       and before reading scanline headers it likewise checks `offset + 8 <= size`.  
       After that it computes `data_size = size - (offset + header_bytes)` and enforces `data_len <= data_size`.  
       Those checks prevent straightforward buffer-overread or reading past the provided data.  
   • Integer overflow risks  
     – All offset arithmetic is done in unsigned 64-bit or `size_t`, then immediately compared against `size`, so wraparound is unlikely in normal 64-bit builds.  
     – On 32-bit platforms, if `size_t` were 32-bit and `offsets[t]` were a large 64-bit value truncated to 32-bit, there could in theory be an overflow—but `offsets` is already a 64-bit type.  
   • Concurrency / data-race  
     – In the scanline path, `invalid_data` is a shared `bool` set by multiple threads under OpenMP without synchronization.  
       This is a classic data‐race: one thread may clear it while another sets it, leading to nondeterministic outcomes.  
       In the worst case a genuine error could be silently ignored.  
   • Memory management  
     – On early returns (invalid data or unsupported features), some allocations (e.g. `tiles` or `images`) are never freed, leading to potential memory leaks if the caller does not clean up.  
   • Unsupported features  
     – The code explicitly rejects Level‐of‐Detail (LoD) tiles (nonzero `level_x`, `level_y`), so malformed or advanced EXR files using LoDs simply error out—no exploitable path is introduced here.  

   Overall, bounds checks around the data pointer and length fields strongly mitigate buffer‐overread/overflow attacks.  The main residual issues are a benign (but correctness-affecting) data race on `invalid_data` under OpenMP and potential leaks on error paths.  

3. Decision  
   No, the core decode loops do not contain straightforward buffer‐overflow or underflow vulnerabilities thanks to explicit bounds checks (though there is a minor data‐race on `invalid_data` under OpenMP and some cleanup omissions on error).

original_information.cve_description: Internally libssl in OpenSSL calls X509_verify_cert() on the client side to verify a certificate supplied by a server. That function may return a negative return value to indicate an internal error (for example out of memory). Such a negative return value is mishandled by OpenSSL and will cause an IO function (such as SSL_connect() or SSL_do_handshake()) to not indicate success and a subsequent call to SSL_get_error() to return the value SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY. This return value is only supposed to be returned by OpenSSL if the application has previously called SSL_CTX_set_cert_verify_callback(). Since most applications do not do this the SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY return value from SSL_get_error() will be totally unexpected and applications may not behave correctly as a result. The exact behaviour will depend on the application but it could result in crashes, infinite loops or other similar incorrect responses. This issue is made more serious in combination with a separate bug in OpenSSL 3.0 that will cause X509_verify_cert() to indicate an internal error when processing a certificate chain. This will occur where a certificate does not include the Subject Alternative Name extension but where a Certificate Authority has enforced name constraints. This issue can occur even with valid chains. By combining the two issues an attacker could induce incorrect, application dependent behaviour. Fixed in OpenSSL 3.0.1 (Affected 3.0.0).
original_information.commit_msg:
Fix invalid handling of verify errors in libssl

In the event that X509_verify() returned an internal error result then
libssl would mishandle this and set rwstate to SSL_RETRY_VERIFY. This
subsequently causes SSL_get_error() to return SSL_ERROR_WANT_RETRY_VERIFY.
That return code is supposed to only ever be returned if an application
is using an app verify callback to complete replace the use of
X509_verify(). Applications may not be written to expect that return code
and could therefore crash (or misbehave in some other way) as a result.

The function `seq_parameter_set::read` parses a Sequence Parameter Set (SPS) from an HEVC bitstream. In order, it:

• Reads the Video Parameter Set ID (4 bits) and the maximum number of temporal sublayers (3 bits + 1), enforcing a maximum of 7 sublayers.  
• Reads the temporal ID nesting flag (1 bit) and passes control to `profile_tier_level_.read` to parse profile/tier info for the specified number of sublayers.  
• Reads the SPS ID as an unsigned VLC and bounds-checks it against the maximum allowed SPS count.  
• Parses the chroma format (VLC). If format = 3, reads a “separate colour plane” flag, then validates that the chroma format is in [0,3].  
• Reads picture dimensions (width and height in luma samples, VLC) and checks they are non-zero and under implementation limits.  
• Reads a conformance-window flag; if set, reads left/right/top/bottom offsets (VLC), otherwise zeroes them.  
• Reads luma and chroma bit-depths as VLC + 8, and ensures neither exceeds 16 bits.  
• Reads `log2_max_pic_order_cnt_lsb` as VLC + 4, checks it lies in [4,16], and computes `MaxPicOrderCntLsb = 1 << that_value`.  
• Parses sub-layer ordering info: a flag selects whether to repeat parameters for all sublayers or only the last. For each sublayer, it reads:  
  – `sps_max_dec_pic_buffering` via UVLC, checks `+1 <= MAX_NUM_REF_PICS`.  
  – `sps_max_num_reorder_pics` (VLC)  
  – `sps_max_latency_increase_plus1` (VLC), and computes `SpsMaxLatencyPictures`.  
  If only the final layer was specified, it then copies those values to earlier layers.  
• Reads transform block size and hierarchy parameters (various VLC or VLC+offset calls), enforcing maximums.  
• Reads flags for scaling lists; if enabled and data present, calls `read_scaling_list`, otherwise sets defaults.  
• Reads flags for AMP, SAO, and PCM; if PCM is enabled, reads PCM-specific bit-depths and block sizes, disables loop filtering if set, and checks PCM bit-depths do not exceed the picture bit-depths.  
• Reads the number of short-term reference picture sets (UVLC), checks it is ≤64, resizes the `ref_pic_sets` vector, and invokes `read_short_term_ref_pic_set` for each.  
• Reads a flag for long-term reference pics; if set, reads their count (VLC), bounds it by `MAX_NUM_LT_REF_PICS_SPS`, then for each reads a POC LSB (fixed bits) and a “used by current pic” flag.  
• Reads flags for temporal MVP and strong intra smoothing.  
• Reads optional VUI parameters via `vui.read` if present.  
• Reads SPS extension flags for range and multilayer extensions; if range extensions are flagged, calls `range_extension.read`.  
• Calls `compute_derived_values()` to finalize any dependent fields, marks the SPS as read, and returns `DE265_OK` on success or an error code if any check fails.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

• Array and index bounds:  
  – `sps_max_sub_layers` is capped at 7, matching array sizes for per-sublayer parameters.  
  – SPS IDs are checked against `DE265_MAX_SPS_SETS`.  
  – Chroma format, picture dimensions, bit depths, POC LSB bit width, short-term set count (≤64), and long-term set count (≤ `MAX_NUM_LT_REF_PICS_SPS`) are all explicitly range-checked.  
  – Vectors (`ref_pic_sets`) are resized before use; per-element reads are in-bounds.  

• Integer overflows:  
  – All shift and addition operations (e.g., `1 << log2_max_pic_order_cnt_lsb`) have operands in safe bounds (4–16).  
  – VLC offsets add small constants well below 32-bit overflow thresholds.  

• Resource exhaustion:  
  – The only dynamic allocation is `ref_pic_sets.resize(num_short_term_ref_pic_sets)`, where `num_short_term_ref_pic_sets` is capped at 64—too small to exhaust memory.  

• Error handling:

- It starts by pointing `p_data` at the first data byte in the buffer and reading the two-byte MX header (EA, C/R, type, and length).  
  - It rejects any buffer shorter than 2 bytes.  
  - It extracts the “EA” flag, the Command/Response bit (`cr`), and the 4-bit frame type.  
  - It then reads the length field, which may be one or two bytes (as indicated by the EA bit).  

- It compares the decoded length (`mx_len`) to the number of remaining bytes in the buffer.  If they do not match, the frame is considered malformed and dropped.

- Having validated the header, it switches on the frame type (`p_rx_frame->type`) to parse the body of well-formed frames:  
  • PN (Parameter Negotiation)  
  • TEST  
  • FCON/FCOFF (Flow on/Flow off)  
  • MSC (Modem Status Command)  
  • NSC (Non‐Supported Command)  
  • RPN (Remote Port Negotiation)  
  • RLS (Remote Line Status)  

  For each known type it:  
   – Verifies that the remaining length exactly matches the fixed length required for that command.  
   – Parses fields out of the buffer in sequence.  
   – Frees (or re-uses, in the TEST case) the buffer and calls the higher-level handler (`rfc_process_pn()`, `rfc_send_test()`, `rfc_process_test_rsp()`, etc.).  

- If the frame type is unrecognized or the length is wrong, it frees the buffer and, if the message was a command, sends a generic “Non‐Supported Command” (NSC) response.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Bounds Checking  
  The code checks:  
  • `length < 2` up front to avoid under‐running the header.  
  • After reading each header byte, it decrements `length` and refuses to parse further if `length` would go negative.  
  • It computes `mx_len` (the claimed payload length) from one or two length bytes and then compares it exactly to the bytes remaining (`length`).  

  This precludes buffer overruns when pulling fields out of `p_data`.

- Integer Handling  
  • `length` is a 16-bit unsigned and is only decremented after checks, so it cannot underflow before use.  
  • `mx_len` is an 8-bit value constructed in accordance with the RFCOMM variable-length scheme; if a two-byte length is present, the EA bit must be clear on the first byte, forcing a second byte.  

- Memory Safety  
  • The function only ever reads within the declared length of the `BT_HDR` buffer.  
  • On any error path or after processing, the buffer is freed exactly once (or in the TEST case, reused in a controlled way).  
  • There is no use‐after‐free, double‐free, or risky pointer arithmetic beyond the controlled parsing of a linear buffer.  

- No Denial-of-Service by Overlong Frames  
  Frames whose declared length is larger than the buffer are dropped.  Overly large frames are never blindly copied or reassembled into fixed-size stacks.

Conclusion: The code rigorously checks header and length fields before accessing payload bytes.  There are no unchecked pointer advances or unsafe loops.  It cleanly aborts on any mismatch and never reads or writes past the buffer bounds.

3. Decision

No, the code is not vulnerable. It implements proper length checks, honors the RFCOMM EA bits for single- or multi-byte lengths, and never reads beyond the declared buffer.

original_information.commit_message:
net: rework recvmsg handler msg_name and msg_namelen logic

This patch now always passes msg->msg_namelen as 0. recvmsg handlers must
set msg_namelen to the proper size <= sizeof(struct sockaddr_storage)
to return msg_name to the user.

This prevents numerous uninitialized memory leaks we had in the
recvmsg handlers and makes it harder for new code to accidentally leak
uninitialized memory.

Optimize for the case recvfrom is called with NULL as address. We don't
need to copy the address at all, so set it to NULL before invoking the
recvmsg handler. We can do so, because all the recvmsg handlers must
cope with the case a plain read() is called on them. read() also sets
msg_name to NULL.

Also document these changes in include/linux/net.h as suggested by David
Miller.

Changes since RFC:

Set msg->msg_name = NULL if user specified a NULL in msg_name but had a
non-null msg_namelen in verify_iovec/verify_compat_iovec. This doesn't
affect sendto as it would bail out earlier while trying to copy-in the
address. It also more naturally reflects the logic by the callers of
verify_iovec.

With this change in place I could remove "
if (!uaddr || msg_sys->msg_namelen == 0)
	msg->msg_name = NULL
".

This change does not alter the user visible error logic as we ignore
msg_namelen as long as msg_name is NULL.

Also remove two unnecessary curly brackets in ___sys_recvmsg and change
comments to netdev style.

1. Functional Analysis

The function `parse_rock_ridge_inode_internal` parses Rock Ridge extensions in an ISO-9660 directory entry and applies the metadata to a Linux inode.  Here is a high-level breakdown:

•  Initialization  
   –  Check whether Rock Ridge support is enabled for the filesystem (`s_rock`).  
   –  Initialize a `rock_state` structure (`rs`) that holds a copy of the directory-record data and a cursor/length for parsing.  
   –  If extended attribute skipping (`RR_REGARD_XA`) is requested, skip a 14-byte XA header.

•  Main parsing loop (`repeat` / `while (rs.len > 2)`)  
   –  Read the next Rock Ridge entry header (`rr`), which has a one-byte length field and a two-byte signature.  
   –  Reject or abort if the length is out of range (< 3) or if the entry would run past the end of the buffer (`rock_check_overflow`).  
   –  Advance the parse cursor by `rr->len` bytes and reduce `rs.len` accordingly.  
   –  Switch on the two-character signature and handle each case:  
     ·  “SP” (System Use Padding) – verify the continuation header.  
     ·  “CE” (Continuation Area) – record where the rest of the Rock Ridge data continues.  
     ·  “ER” (Extension Reference) – log the extension identifier (e.g. “RRIP_1991A”).  
     ·  “PX” – file permissions, link count, UID/GID → set `inode->i_mode`, `i_uid`, `i_gid`, `i_nlink`.  
     ·  “PN” – device numbers for special files → construct `inode->i_rdev`.  
     ·  “TF” – time fields (create/modify/access/attr) → set `inode->i_{atime,mtime,ctime}`.  
     ·  “SL” – symbolic link components → scan each `SL_component`, compute the total symlink length and store it in `inode->i_size`.  
     ·  “CL” – child relocations for moved directories → re-read the real directory inode (`isofs_iget_reloc`), then copy its metadata into `inode`.  
     ·  “ZF” (if `CONFIG_ZISOFS`) – compressed file info → record compression algorithm and sizes in private fields, adjust `inode->i_size`.  
   –  Unrecognized signatures are ignored.

•  Continuation handling  
   –  When the end of the current buffer is reached, call `rock_continue(&rs)`.  
   –  If there is a continuation area, refill the buffer and resume parsing (`goto repeat`).  

•  Cleanup and return  
   –  Free the buffer held by `rs`.  
   –  Return 0 on success or a negative error code on I/O failure or unsupported recursion.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

A careful review of the code shows that it takes multiple precautions against out-of-bounds access and malformed Rock Ridge records:

•  Length checks  
   –  Each SU (System Use) entry has a one-byte `len` field.  The code rejects lengths < 3 and aborts parsing if consuming `rr->len` would exceed the remaining buffer (`rs.len`).  
   –  After advancing `rs.chr` by `rr->len`, it rechecks that `rs.len` has not gone negative.  

•  Overflow protection  
   –  The helper `rock_check_overflow` (called before consuming the entry) ensures that accessing the `rr` structure and its payload won’t cross the buffer boundary.  

•  Controlled pointer arithmetic  
   –  All advances of `rs.chr` and subtraction from `rs.len` are done only after the overflow checks.  
   –  In the “SL” (symlink) case, a local counter `slen` tracks remaining bytes in that entry, and each component’s `len` is subtracted from `slen` before use.  The loop stops when `slen` drops below the minimum component header size.  

•  No unbounded loops  
   –  The outer `while (rs.len > 2)` and the inner symlink loop both have clear exit conditions based on length counters.  

•  Integer overflow concerns  
   –  Symlink length accumulation is done with signed or unsigned 64-bit fields (`i_size` is `loff_t`), and worst-case symlinks are limited by the size of directory records (max 255 bytes per SU entry).  Thus there is no realistic wraparound.  

•  Error paths  
   –  On malformed data or detected overflow, the code either aborts gracefully (`goto out`) or returns `-EIO` (`goto eio`), but it never dereferences invalid pointers.  

In summary, the code applies standard checks on every parsed SU record, validates lengths before accessing memory, tracks remaining buffer space, and handles all error paths with cleanups. No unguarded pointer arithmetic or unchecked lengths are visible.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a buffer-overflow or similar vulnerability. It robustly validates all length fields, prevents over-reads via `rock_check_overflow`, and uses intra-entry length counters in every parsing loop.

original_information.Summary: The parse_rock_ridge_inode_internal function in fs/isofs/rock.c in the Linux kernel through 3.16.1 allows local users to cause a denial of service (unkillable mount process) via a crafted iso9660 image with a self-referential CL entry.
original_information.commit_message:
isofs: Fix unbounded recursion when processing relocated directories

We did not check relocated directory in any way when processing Rock
Ridge 'CL' tag. Thus a corrupted isofs image can possibly have a CL
entry pointing to another CL entry leading to possibly unbounded
recursion in kernel code and thus stack overflow or deadlocks (if there
is a loop created from CL entries).

Fix the problem by not allowing CL entry to point to a directory entry
with CL entry (such use makes no good sense anyway) and by checking
whether CL entry doesn't point to itself.

Reported-by: Chris Evans <cevans@google.com>

original_information.cve_description: An issue was discovered in Xen through 4.12.x allowing 32-bit PV guest OS users to gain guest OS privileges by installing and using descriptors. There is missing descriptor table limit checking in x86 PV emulation. When emulating certain PV guest operations, descriptor table accesses are performed by the emulating code. Such accesses should respect the guest specified limits, unless otherwise guaranteed to fail in such a case. Without this, emulation of 32-bit guest user mode calls through call gates would allow guest user mode to install and then use descriptors of their choice, as long as the guest kernel did not itself install an LDT. (Most OSes don't install any LDT by default). 32-bit PV guest user mode can elevate its privileges to that of the guest kernel. Xen versions from at least 3.2 onwards are affected. Only 32-bit PV guest user mode can leverage this vulnerability. HVM, PVH, as well as 64-bit PV guests cannot leverage this vulnerability. Arm systems are unaffected.
original_information.commit_msg:
x86/PV: check GDT/LDT limits during emulation

Accesses beyond the LDT limit originating from emulation would trigger
the ASSERT() in pv_map_ldt_shadow_page(). On production builds such
accesses would cause an attempt to promote the touched page (offset from
the present LDT base address) to a segment descriptor one. If this
happens to succeed, guest user mode would be able to elevate its
privileges to that of the guest kernel. This is particularly easy when
there's no LDT at all, in which case the LDT base stored internally to
Xen is simply zero.

Also adjust the ASSERT() that was triggering: It was off by one to
begin with, and for production builds we also better use
ASSERT_UNREACHABLE() instead with suitable recovery code afterwards.

This is XSA-298.

Reported-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>
Signed-off-by: Jan Beulich <jbeulich@suse.com>
Reviewed-by: Andrew Cooper <andrew.cooper3@citrix.com>

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `http_parse_cont_len_header` takes:  
  • `value`: an `ist` struct holding a pointer/length pair for the header’s raw value.  
  • `body_len`: a pointer to an unsigned‐long‐long to receive the parsed length.  
  • `not_first`: a flag indicating whether this is a subsequent Content-Length header in the request.  

- It initializes:  
  • `word` to point at the same buffer as `value`.  
  • `e` to point one past the end of the buffer.  
  • `check_prev` to `not_first`, so that if this is not the first header, any new length must match the old one.  

- It then enters a loop to parse one (or a comma-separated list of) decimal integers:  
  1. Skip any leading linear whitespace (LWS).  
  2. If we reach the end before seeing a digit, fail.  
  3. Parse a run of digits into `cl`, checking at each step for:  
     – overflow on multiply by 10 (`cl > ULLONG_MAX/10`)  
     – overflow on add (`cl + c < cl`)  
     If any non‐digit appears immediately, or we detect overflow, we fail.  
  4. Record the exact substring of digits in `word.len = n - word.ptr`.  
  5. Skip any trailing LWS. If the next non‐LWS is a comma, consume it and loop to parse the next number; if it’s end‐of‐buffer, we’re done. Otherwise fail.  
  6. If this isn’t the first header (`check_prev`=1) and the newly parsed `cl` differs from `*body_len`, fail.  
  7. Store `cl` into `*body_len` and store `word` back into `*value`.  
  8. On exit from the loop, return `1` if this was the first header (so it should be indexed) or `0` if it was a duplicate.

- On any malformed input or overflow, the code jumps to `fail` and returns –1.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Integer-overflow: The code explicitly checks before multiplying by 10 and before adding the digit, so it cannot overflow `unsigned long long`.  
- Buffer-over‐read/under‐read: All pointer walks (`word.ptr` and `n`) are bounded by `e = ptr+len`. The code always checks `< e` before dereferencing.  
- Invalid characters: Any non‐digit in the digit span (or any non‐comma non‐LWS after) causes an immediate failure.  
- Multiple headers: If more than one Content-Length header is present, any differing values cause failure (`check_prev`).  
- Leading/trailing whitespace and comma lists are handled precisely per HTTP specs.  

No unchecked memory writes, no format‐string abuse, no integer or buffer overflow, no policy bypass. The function rejects any malformed or malicious variation.

3. Decision

No, based on the bounds checks, overflow checks, and strict character validation, the code contains no identifiable vulnerabilities.

original_information.commit_msg:
BUG/MAJOR: http: reject any empty content-length header value

The content-length header parser has its dedicated function, in order
to take extreme care about invalid, unparsable, or conflicting values.
But there's a corner case in it, by which it stops comparing values
when reaching the end of the header. This has for a side effect that
an empty value or a value that ends with a comma does not deserve
further analysis, and it acts as if the header was absent.

While this is not necessarily a problem for the value ending with a
comma as it will be cause a header folding and will disappear, it is a
problem for the first isolated empty header because this one will not
be recontructed when next ones are seen, and will be passed as-is to the
backend server. A vulnerable HTTP/1 server hosted behind haproxy that
would just use this first value as "0" and ignore the valid one would
then not be protected by haproxy and could be attacked this way, taking
the payload for an extra request.

In field the risk depends on the server. Most commonly used servers
already have safe content-length parsers, but users relying on haproxy
to protect a known-vulnerable server might be at risk (and the risk of
a bug even in a reputable server should never be dismissed).

A configuration-based work-around consists in adding the following rule
in the frontend, to explicitly reject requests featuring an empty
content-length header that would have not be folded into an existing
one:

    http-request deny if { hdr_len(content-length) 0 }

The real fix consists in adjusting the parser so that it always expects a
value at the beginning of the header or after a comma. It will now reject
requests and responses having empty values anywhere in the C-L header.

This needs to be backported to all supported versions. Note that the
modification was made to functions h1_parse_cont_len_header() and
http_parse_cont_len_header(). Prior to 2.8 the latter was in
h2_parse_cont_len_header(). One day the two should be refused but the
former is also used by Lua.

The HTTP messaging reg-tests were completed to test these cases.

Thanks to Ben Kallus of Dartmouth College and Narf Industries for
reporting this! (this is in GH #2237).

original_information.commit_msg:
Use correct origin when prompting for proxy authentication.

Since M49, Chrome has been prompting for proxy authentication
credentials using the target origin instead of the origin of the proxy
server. Even if the proxy origin was displayed correctly, a mischievous
network operator could still spoof the proxy server origin. To mitigate
these problems, this CL:

* Fixes the origin used in the proxy authentication login prompt to use
  the origin of the proxy server.

* Indicate if the proxy server connection is insecure.

* Always throw up an interstitial and clear the omnibox when showing a
  proxy auth prompt.

* Use the correct origin when saving proxy authentication credentials.

1. Functional Analysis

  - The function `cherokee_validator_parse_basic` takes a `validator` struct pointer, a pointer `str` to a Base64-encoded credential blob, and its length `str_len`.  
  - It first guards against a null or zero-length input, bailing out on error.  
  - It appends the raw Base64 data into a temporary `auth` buffer and then decodes that buffer in place.  
  - It searches the decoded data for the first colon (`:`), which separates username from password in HTTP Basic auth. If no colon is found, it treats the input as malformed.  
  - It splits the decoded buffer at the colon, copying the bytes before the colon into `validator->user` and the bytes after into `validator->passwd`.  
  - On success it logs the discovered user and password, frees the temporary buffer, and returns success; on any error it frees the buffer and returns an error code.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  - No unchecked buffers: all data additions go through `cherokee_buffer_add`, which is assumed to manage its own allocations and bounds. The code never writes past the end of any buffer.  
  - Malformed/invalid Base64: the code does not check a return value from `cherokee_buffer_decode_base64`. If that routine leaves the buffer in a partially decoded or corrupted state, the colon scan could misbehave or the split may copy invalid data. In practice the decoder should reject non-Base64 input or sanitize it, but this function makes no explicit check.  
  - Resource exhaustion (DoS): there is no upper bound on `str_len`. An attacker could supply an extremely long Base64 string, forcing large heap allocations during `buffer_add` or `buffer_decode_base64`, leading to memory exhaustion or slowdown.  
  - Null-termination: the code relies on the buffer implementation to present a NUL-terminated `auth.buf` (for `strchr` and later `%s` printing). If the buffer is not NUL-terminated after decode, `strchr` or the `TRACE` call could read out of bounds.  
  - Injection risks: the parser itself does no sanitization of user or password contents beyond splitting at the colon. Any downstream use of these values (e.g., in SQL or shell contexts) must perform its own escaping or validation.

3. Decision

No, the parser does not contain an immediate memory‐corruption or overflow vulnerability, but it lacks explicit error checking on Base64 decoding, imposes no maximum length on input (allowing potential DoS), and assumes NUL termination.

1. Functional Analysis

- Definition  
  The function `_pyfribidi_log2vis` is a Python C-extension entry point that wraps a reordering routine. It accepts keyword arguments and invokes an underlying bidirectional-visualization function.

- Argument parsing  
  - Uses `PyArg_ParseTupleAndKeywords` with format `"U|iii"`, meaning:  
    1. A required Python Unicode object (`logical`).  
    2. Optional integers for `base_direction` (`base`), `clean`, and `reordernsm`.  
  - Default values are set before parsing:  
    • `base = FRIBIDI_TYPE_RTL`  
    • `clean = 0`  
    • `reordernsm = 1`

- Base‐direction validation  
  After parsing, the code checks that `base` matches one of the three allowed FriBidi paragraph types: `FRIBIDI_TYPE_RTL`, `FRIBIDI_TYPE_LTR`, or `FRIBIDI_TYPE_ON`. If it does not, it raises a `ValueError`.

- Core functionality  
  Finally, it calls `unicode_log2vis(logical, base, clean, reordernsm)`, returning its result (presumably a new Python Unicode object containing the visually reordered string).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Argument parsing safety  
  `PyArg_ParseTupleAndKeywords` with format `"U|iii"` ensures the first argument is a properly-typed Unicode object, and extracts three integers. It does not perform any unchecked buffer operations or direct pointer arithmetic.

- Integer validation  
  Only `base` is range‐checked. The flags `clean` and `reordernsm` are taken as raw integers (no explicit 0/1 bounds), but they are then passed to `unicode_log2vis`. Without seeing `unicode_log2vis`, one cannot categorically claim misuse, but in typical FriBidi usage these flags are interpreted as boolean, so out‐of‐range values should have no adverse effect beyond logical “true/false.”

- Memory safety  
  No manual `malloc`/`free` or raw pointer arithmetic is done here. The code relies on the Python C-API and likely safe idioms in `unicode_log2vis`. If `unicode_log2vis` itself is implemented correctly, there is no memory corruption or buffer overflow exposure in this wrapper.

- Error handling  
  Parsing failures and invalid `base` values correctly propagate Python exceptions. There are no silent fails or unchecked error returns.

3. Decision

No, this code snippet does not itself contain any vulnerabilities.

original_information.commit_message:
refactor pyfribidi.c module

pyfribidi.c is now compiled as _pyfribidi. This module only handles
unicode internally and doesn't use the fribidi_utf8_to_unicode
function (which can't handle 4 byte utf-8 sequences). This fixes the
buffer overflow in issue #2.

The code is now also much simpler: pyfribidi.c is down from 280 to 130
lines of code.

We now ship a pure python pyfribidi that handles the case when
non-unicode strings are passed in.

We now also adapt the size of the output string if clean=True is
passed.

+"""simple Python binding for fribidi.
+
+pyfribidi uses libfribidi to order text visually using the unicode
+algorithm. pyfribidi can also convert text from visual order to
+logical order, but the conversion may be wrong in certain cases.

+
+from _pyfribidi import LTR, ON, RTL, log2vis as _log2vis
+
+def log2vis(logical, base_direction=RTL, encoding="utf-8", clean=False, reordernsm=True):
+    """
+    Return string reordered visually according to base direction.
+    Return the same type of input string, either unicode or string using
+    encoding.
+
+    Note that this function does not handle line breaking. You should
+    call log2vis with each line.
+
+    Arguments:
+    - logical: unicode or encoded string
+    - base_direction: optional logical base direction. Accepts one of
+      the constants LTR, RTL or ON, defined in this module. ON calculate
+      the base direction according to the BiDi algorithm.
+    - encoding: optional string encoding (ignored for unicode input)
+    """
+
+    if not isinstance(logical, unicode):
+        logical = unicode(logical, encoding)
+    else:
+        encoding = None
+    res = _log2vis(logical, base_direction=base_direction, clean=clean, reordernsm=reordernsm)
+    if encoding:
+        return res.encode(encoding)

1. Functional Analysis

- The method `MetaDataBase::dumpToLog() const` acquires a lock on `mInternalData->mLock` via `std::lock_guard` to ensure thread‐safe access to the internal data.
- It then iterates backwards over all entries in `mInternalData->mItems`.
- For each entry:
  - It retrieves the 32‐bit key (`keyAt(i)`).
  - It formats that key into a four‐character code string in a 5‐byte buffer (`char cc[5]`) via `MakeFourCCString`.
  - It fetches the corresponding value object (`typed_data &item = valueAt(i)`).
  - It calls `item.asString(true /* verbose */).string()` to get a verbose textual representation.
  - Finally, it logs the key and the stringified value with `ALOGI("%s: %s", cc, …)`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer bounds: `cc[5]` is sized to hold exactly 4 characters plus a null terminator. Assuming `MakeFourCCString` is correctly implemented to write at most 4 chars + NUL, there is no overflow.
- Format‐string safety: The format string `"%s: %s"` is a compile‐time constant, and both `%s` arguments are passed as `char const*`, so there is no format‐string vulnerability.
- Lifetime of temporary string: `item.asString(true)` returns a temporary string object whose `string()` pointer remains valid for the duration of the full expression (i.e., through the `ALOGI` call). Thus the logged pointer is valid when it’s consumed.
- Thread safety: The mutex prevents concurrent modification of `mItems` while dumping.
- No unvalidated user input is used as a format specifier or as unchecked buffer size.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any exploitable vulnerabilities.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `cleanup_pathname` (alias `cleanup_pathname_fsobj`) normalizes an input path string in-place.  
- It first checks for an empty string and reports an error if so.  
- On Cygwin, it calls `cleanup_pathname_win` to handle Windows-style paths.  
- If the path begins with `/`, it optionally rejects absolute paths when the flag `ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NOABSOLUTEPATHS` is set.  
- It then scans the remainder of the string element by element, copying each valid component to the “dest” write pointer while:  
  • Collapsing repeated `/` separators into one.  
  • Skipping `./` segments.  
  • Optionally rejecting any `..` segments if the flag `ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NODOTDOT` is set.  
- It never removes `..` entries from the normalized output when they are allowed; it simply leaves them intact.  
- If nothing was copied (e.g., input was `.` or `/././`), it leaves a single `.` or `/` as the result.  
- Finally, it null-terminates the cleaned path and returns `ARCHIVE_OK`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer Safety: The function writes into the same buffer at most as many bytes as the original string had, so there is no risk of a buffer overflow in normal use  
- Absolute-path rejection: When `ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NOABSOLUTEPATHS` is set, any leading slash triggers an error, preventing absolute‐path extraction.  
- Dot-dot (`..`) handling:  
   • If `ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_NODOTDOT` is set, the function rejects paths containing `..`, preventing directory-traversal attacks.  
   • If that flag is not set, `..` elements are preserved rather than resolved, which can in principle allow directory traversal if the calling code subsequently treats the cleaned path as safe. However, this is by design (the caller must explicitly opt in or out of `..` handling).  
- Windows separators: On Cygwin the code delegates to `cleanup_pathname_win`, which is presumed to handle backslashes. On POSIX builds, backslashes remain untouched but do not affect forward-slash–based normalization.  
- No other side effects, memory leaks, or privilege issues are introduced.

3. Decision

No, the code does not itself contain a vulnerability. It correctly enforces absolute-path and `..` restrictions when the appropriate flags are set, and it avoids buffer overflows by doing in-place, length-preserving normalization.

1. Functional Analysis

- Retrieve the network namespace (`net`) associated with the socket.
- Check the `sysctl_tcp_mtu_probing` setting; if it is 0, abort (probing disabled).
- On the first invocation for a connection (`icsk_mtup.enabled == 0`):  
  • Mark probing enabled.  
  • Record the current time in `probe_timestamp` (for pacing/timeout).  
- On subsequent invocations:  
  • Take the previous probe’s MTU hint (`search_low`), convert it to an MSS, and halve it.  
  • Clamp that MSS to at most `sysctl_tcp_base_mss`.  
  • Clamp downwards to at least the minimum IPv4 packet payload (68 bytes minus header).  
  • Also enforce the configured `sysctl_tcp_min_snd_mss`.  
  • Convert the final MSS back into an MTU, storing it in `search_low` for the next probe.  
- Call `tcp_sync_mss()` to apply the newly computed (or initial) PMTU/MSS settings to the socket.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Integer arithmetic: all intermediate values are clamped by well-defined min/max operations; there is no unbounded addition or multiplication that could overflow in a dangerous way.  
- No pointer arithmetic or buffer writes occur here, so there is no risk of buffer overflows.  
- All inputs (sysctls, stored MTU/MSS values) are validated or clamped before use, preventing out-of-range values.  
- The logic is gated by a sysctl flag, so an attacker cannot force it to run unless probing is explicitly enabled by an administrator.  
- There are no unchecked loops or recursion; the function executes in bounded time.

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It safely computes and clamps MTU/MSS values before applying them.

original_information.cve_description: Jonathan Looney discovered that the Linux kernel default MSS is hard-coded to 48 bytes. This allows a remote peer to fragment TCP resend queues significantly more than if a larger MSS were enforced. A remote attacker could use this to cause a denial of service. This has been fixed in stable kernel releases 4.4.182, 4.9.182, 4.14.127, 4.19.52, 5.1.11, and is fixed in commits 967c05aee439e6e5d7d805e195b3a20ef5c433d6 and 5f3e2bf008c2221478101ee72f5cb4654b9fc363.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `dissect_application_isup` is a Wireshark dissector callback for the “application/ISUP” media type.  
- It declares local variables for a protocol tree item (`ti`), a subtree (`isup_tree`), a sub-buffer (`message_tvb`), the ISUP message type byte (`message_type`), two parameter strings (`version`, `base`), and a variant selector (`itu_isup_variant`, defaulting to the ITU standard).  
- If `data` is non‐NULL, it is cast to an HTTP‐message info struct and the code looks for MIME parameters named “version” and “base” in `media_str`.  
  - If either parameter begins with “ansi” (case‐insensitive, up to 4 bytes), the routine:  
    • Sets a global (or file‐scope) `isup_standard` flag to `ANSI_STANDARD`.  
    • Updates the protocol and info columns to show “ISUP(ANSI)” and the ANSI message-type acronym.  
    • Adds an ISUP subtree to the packet details tree (if `tree` is provided).  
    • Slices the entire TVB into `message_tvb` and calls `dissect_ansi_isup_message`.  
    • Frees the temporary `version`/`base` strings and returns.  
  - Else if “spirou” is found, it sets the variant to `ISUP_FRENCH_VARIANT`; otherwise it leaves the standard at ITU.  In all cases it frees `version` and `base`.  
- After that conditional block (or immediately if `data`/`media_str` was NULL), the first byte of `tvb` is read into `message_type`.  
- A `switch` on `itu_isup_variant` then chooses how to label the protocol/info columns (ITU, French, or a default “unknown variant”).  
- If a tree pointer was passed in, an ISUP subtree is added.  
- Finally, the code creates `message_tvb` as the subset of the original TVB from offset 0 onward, calls `dissect_isup_message` with the selected variant, and returns the full length of the original TVB.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer accesses  
  • All reads from the packet buffer are done via Wireshark’s `tvb_get_guint8` and `tvb_new_subset_remaining` APIs, which perform internal bounds checking. There is no raw pointer arithmetic or unguarded indexing, so out‐of‐bounds reads are prevented.  
- String handling  
  • The code uses `ws_find_media_type_parameter`, which returns newly allocated NUL‐terminated strings or NULL, and then compares them by `g_ascii_strncasecmp`/`g_ascii_strcasecmp`. These Glib functions safely stop at a NUL and never overrun.  
  • Both `version` and `base` are `g_free`d in every control path after use; `g_free(NULL)` is a no‐op. There is no double‐free or use‐after‐free.  
- Format strings  
  • Column updates use `col_append_*_fstr` with format specifiers matched to the data. There is no user‐controlled format string injection.  
- Global state  
  • The code writes a global (or file‐scope) `isup_standard` variable, which may affect other dissections if used concurrently. Wireshark is essentially single‐threaded per‐capture‐file during dissection, so this is not ordinarily a thread‐safety risk.  
- Error paths  
  • If `data` or `media_str` is NULL, or if the TVB is too short, the code defaults cleanly to the ITU variant and still calls the generic dissector. No crashes or memory corruption should occur.

Conclusion: there are no unchecked raw buffer accesses, no unsafe string or memory operations, and no format‐string or integer‐overflow issues. The code follows Wireshark’s safe‐API patterns.

3. Decision

No, I found no exploitable vulnerabilities in this code.

1. Functional Analysis  
   
   The function ieee80211_rx_h_decrypt() is called during frame reception in the mac80211 stack. Its high-level steps are:  
   A. Initial checks  
      – If the frame is “extended” (802.11w Protected Management Frames in the extensible header) it bails out with RX_CONTINUE (no further decryption here).  
      – It extracts the 802.11 header, RX status, and figures out whether the frame was marked as already IV‐stripped by the driver.  
   B. PTK (pairwise) key lookup  
      – If we have an associated station (rx->sta), load the station’s current PTK (based on rx->sta->ptk_idx).  
      – If the frame is protected and the driver did not strip the IV, extract the IV’s key index and pick the corresponding PTK entry for that index.  
   C. MMIE (management MIC) index lookup  
      – If the frame is _not_ marked protected in the FC field, peek for an MMIE key index in management frames (used with BIP).  
   D. Key selection by frame type and addressing  
      – **Unicast data** (addr1 not multicast) and a valid station PTK: pick ptk_idx if present, otherwise the default sta_ptk.  If already decrypted or not protected, skip further decryption.  
      – **Beacon frames** with a valid MMIE index: handle BIP for beacons (“BIGTK”), verify index is in the beacon‐key range, load the beacon key. If it isn’t set, return RX_CONTINUE so the frame can be passed as unprotected.  
      – **Other group management (multicast) frames with MMIE**: validate MMIE index in the group-management BIP range, then look up the GTK in link_sta or link; fall back to link->gtk if station did not store a per-station GTK.  
      – **Completely unprotected frames** (IEEE80211_HAS_PROTECTED bit off): find any GTK or default‐mgmt key that _would_ have been used if protection were expected, stash that in rx->key (so that we can later drop frames that arrive unprotected when protection was mandated), then return RX_CONTINUE (no decryption).  
      – **Driver-stripped IV for protected frames**: the IV is gone, so the function can’t automatically pick the right key. It then extracts keyid from the raw skb, and indexes into per-station GTK, link GTK, or the driver’s default keys array (sdata->keys).  Non-WEP unicast with only GTK/IGTK indices is rejected.  
   E. Key flag checks  
      – If rx->key is set and KEY_FLAG_TAINTED is present, the frame is dropped (RX_DROP_MONITOR).  
      – If rx->key is still NULL, the frame is dropped (RX_DROP_MONITOR).  
   F. Decryption dispatch  
      – Based on rx->key->conf.cipher, call the appropriate decryption routine: WEP, TKIP, CCMP, CCMP-256, AES-CMAC (BIP), AES-CMAC_256 (BIP-256), AES-GMAC, GCMP, etc.  
   G. Post-decrypt bookkeeping  
      – Mark RX_FLAG_DECRYPTED in status->flag so that upper layers know decryption was attempted.  
      – If decrypt fails badly for a beacon, notify cfg80211 that an unprotected management frame arrived when protection was expected.  
   H. Return the RX handling result (RX_CONTINUE, RX_DROP_UNUSABLE, RX_DROP_MONITOR, or RX_DROP_KEY).

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   
   a. Array‐index safety  
      – Key indices are extracted either from 2-bit fields in the IV or from the MMIE header. Both sources are constrained by protocol (“keyid” fields in the IV are 0–3, MMIE key indices are validated against known ranges before indexing).  
      – Lookups into gtk[keyidx] or default key arrays check that keyidx lies in the expected range. There is no unchecked out-of-bounds array indexing.  
   b. NULL and error handling  
      – If no suitable key is found, the code consistently returns a drop or continue code that does not perform decryption, so there is no uncontrolled pointer dereference.  
   c. Replay or nonce misuse  
      – This function does not manage counters or nonce replays directly; it simply dispatches to the crypto code, which maintains counters and verifies MICs. No bypass of those checks is apparent.  
   d. Race conditions and memory safety  
      – Key pointers are read under RCU (`rcu_dereference()`), so they remain valid during the critical sections of key lookup and before the RCU grace period. There is no use‐after‐free or double‐free.  
   e. Cipher-specific weaknesses  
      – WEP and TKIP are inherently insecure, but the code’s role is purely to decrypt or reject; it does not worsen those weaknesses.  
   f. Policy enforcement  
      – Unprotected frames arriving when protection was expected (e.g., data frames under RSNA) get dropped or notified correctly. Management‐frame protection (BIP) is validated via MMIE indexes in bounds.  
   
   There is no evidence of a buffer overflow, integer overflow, unchecked pointer dereference, race condition, or bypass of replay/MIC checks. All protocol fields used for indexing are range-checked, and the dispatch to the cipher implementations follows after a key is verified non-NULL and not tainted.

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain a readily exploitable vulnerability. It correctly selects, bounds-checks, and validates the cryptographic key entries, and rejects frames that cannot be safely decrypted or whose protection policies would be violated.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function begins by parsing a small header from `s->buf` to extract the sub-rectangle’s position (`frame_x`, `frame_y`) and size (`frame_width`, `frame_height`) within the overall video frame.
- It then adjusts these coordinates by any previously saved offsets (`s->x_off`, `s->y_off`), and validates that the resulting rectangle is fully inside the codec’s target frame buffer.
- If the update region does not cover the full frame, it copies the previous frame’s pixels into the new frame buffer so that unchanged areas are preserved.
- Next, if the header bit 0x02 is set, it reads a new 256-entry 24-bit palette (3 bytes per entry), expands each component, and stores it in `s->palette`.
- It reads a “method” byte.  If bit 7 is set, it treats the payload as LZ-compressed, unpacks it into a work buffer via `lz_unpack()`, masks off the compression bit, and reinitializes its input cursor on the unpacked data.
- `dp` and `pp` are set to point at the start of the update rectangle in the current and previous frames, respectively.
- The switch on `meth` implements three decoding modes:
  1. A simple run-length/intra‐frame or inter-frame copy decoder that reads a control byte `len`.  If the high bit of `len` is set it copies `len&0x7F + 1` literal pixels from the bitstream; otherwise it copies `len + 1` pixels from the same position in the previous frame.
  2. A raw-copy mode that simply reads `frame_width` pixels per scanline from the bitstream.
  3. A mixed RLE mode similar to (1) but, on seeing a 0xFF marker in the input, invokes `rle_unpack()` to decode an extra layer of RLE.
- Each scanline is written into `frame->data[0]` (using `linesize[0]` for stride) and references the old frame in `s->prev_frame->data[0]` for inter-frame copies.
- On success, the new frame buffer is populated and the function returns 0.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- The code validates the update rectangle (`frame_x`, `frame_y`, `frame_width`, `frame_height`) against the known frame dimensions, preventing out-of-bounds writes when storing decoded pixels.
- In methods 1 and 3, every time it reads a length `len`, it checks both “does this run fit within the current scanline?” and “are there at least `len` bytes left in the bitstream?” before doing any read or inter-frame `memcpy`.
- When importing a new palette, it verifies that there are at least 256×3 bytes remaining.
- When unpacking LZ data, it fails if the unpack buffer is unset or if `lz_unpack` returns an error.
- The only branch that does not explicitly check “bytes left in the bitstream ≥ frame_width” is method 2, where it calls `bytestream2_get_buffer(&gb, dp, frame_width)`.  In FFmpeg’s bytestream2 API this macro will `memcpy` unconditionally and then advance the read pointer.  If the packet is shorter than expected, this could read past the end of the packet buffer (an out-of-bounds read), which in pathological cases might crash (denial-of-service) but does not write outside the allocated frame buffer.
- All writes into `dp` are bounded by validated `frame_width` and `frame_height`, so there is no direct out-of-bounds write or heap corruption in normal usage.

3. Decision

No,[The code applies bounds checks on coordinates, palette reads, RLE and inter-frame copies, and rejects ill-formed lengths in all but one “raw” branch.  The only weakness is a potential out-of-bounds read in method 2 when the packet is truncated, which at worst can cause a crash but not memory corruption beyond the frame buffer.]

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `dm_table_create` allocates and initializes a new device-mapper table object.  
   - It first checks whether the requested number of targets exceeds a hard limit (`DM_MAX_TARGETS`) and rejects oversized requests.  
   - It allocates zeroed memory for the table structure (`kzalloc`) and initializes its list head and read–write semaphore.  
   - If the caller passed zero targets, it substitutes a default (`KEYS_PER_NODE`) and then rounds the target count up to the next multiple of `KEYS_PER_NODE`.  
   - A second zero check ensures that rounding did not wrap around to zero. If it did, the function frees the structure and returns an overflow error.  
   - It calls `alloc_targets` to reserve internal target slots. On allocation failure it cleans up and returns `-ENOMEM`.  
   - Finally, it sets the table’s type to `DM_TYPE_NONE`, stores the requested mode and the mapped device pointer, returns the new table via `*result`, and returns success (0).

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Integer overflow: The code checks the raw `num_targets` against `DM_MAX_TARGETS` and again verifies that rounding up did not wrap to zero. If `KEYS_PER_NODE` were zero, the rounding logic could misbehave, but the code’s second zero check would catch a nonsensical result.  
   - Memory allocation failures: Every allocation (`kzalloc`, `alloc_targets`) is checked, and on failure the code frees any partially built state before returning.  
   - Use-after-free or double-free: The pointer to the new table is not published until after all initialization is complete, and each early-exit path frees exactly once.  
   - Race conditions: Initialization happens fully before `*result` is assigned; no premature exposure of the object.  
   - No unbounded loops or buffer overruns appear. Any further size computations happen inside `alloc_targets`, which is outside this snippet.  

   Overall, the function includes appropriate bounds checks, error handling, and cleanup. We see no path that leads to resource leaks, out-of-bounds writes, or use-after-free errors here.

3. Decision  
   No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It checks inputs, handles allocation failures, and correctly initializes or tears down internal state.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - Disable quota accounting on umount: f2fs_quota_off_umount(sb)  
   - Prevent further shrinker invocations by locking umount_mutex  
   - If the filesystem is marked dirty or if the previous checkpoint wasn’t done under umount, force a checkpoint:  
     • Prepare cp_control with reason CP_UMOUNT  
     • Call write_checkpoint()  
   - Wait for any in-flight discard (TRIM) I/Os to complete: f2fs_wait_discard_bios(sbi, true)  
   - If discard support is enabled but no blocks have yet been trimmed, issue a final trimmed checkpoint:  
     • Prepare cp_control with CP_UMOUNT | CP_TRIMMED  
     • Call write_checkpoint() again  
   - Tear down internal statistics: f2fs_destroy_stats(sbi)  
   - Release any remaining inode entries (and mark them clean): release_ino_entry(sbi, true)  
   - Leave the shrinker framework: f2fs_leave_shrinker(sbi)  
   - Unlock umount_mutex  
   - Flush any merged writeback buffers: f2fs_flush_merged_writes(sbi)  
   - Drop references to the special node and meta inodes: iput(sbi->node_inode); iput(sbi->meta_inode)  
   - Destroy the node and segment managers: destroy_node_manager(sbi); destroy_segment_manager(sbi)  
   - Free on-disk checkpoint structure: kfree(sbi->ckpt)  
   - Unregister sysfs entries: f2fs_unregister_sysfs(sbi)  
   - Clear the fs-specific pointer in the VFS superblock: sb->s_fs_info = NULL  
   - Free the checksum shash if one was allocated: crypto_free_shash(sbi->s_chksum_driver)  
   - Free the raw-in-memory superblock: kfree(sbi->raw_super)  
   - Tear down device lists, mempool, per-CPU data, quota names, write_io arrays and finally the sbi itself: destroy_device_list, mempool_destroy, destroy_percpu_info, kfree() loops, kfree(sbi)

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Memory safety: All dynamically allocated blocks (ckpt, raw_super, per-CPU info, write_io arrays, the sbi structure itself) are freed exactly once in a well-defined order, and there is no further use of those pointers after free.  
   - Use-after-free: After sb->s_fs_info is nulled out, none of the F2FS teardown paths reference sb->s_fs_info again. The inodes (node_inode and meta_inode) are dropped before the managers that might depend on them are destroyed, avoiding stale references.  
   - Double-free: No object is freed more than once. Conditional frees (e.g. checksum driver) only occur when the object is present.  
   - Concurrency: The umount_mutex protects against simultaneous shrinker callbacks; shrinker is formally removed before unlocking. After unlocking, no remaining background work touches the already-destroyed structures.  
   - Integer overflows or user-controlled size parameters are not in play here—this routine simply frees and tears down.  
   - Error handling: Critical cleanup always runs; even if write_checkpoint is skipped on an I/O error, subsequent resource freeing still occurs so there is no resource leakage.

3. Decision  
   No, this code does not appear to contain any memory-safety or logic vulnerabilities. It follows a correct and consistent teardown sequence, avoids use-after-free and double-free, and properly synchronizes against background work.

original_information.Summary: The f2fs implementation in the Linux kernel before 4.14 mishandles reference counts associated with f2fs_wait_discard_bios calls, which allows local users to cause a denial of service (BUG), as demonstrated by fstrim.
original_information.commit_message:
f2fs: fix potential panic during fstrim

As Ju Hyung Park reported:

"When 'fstrim' is called for manual trim, a BUG() can be triggered
randomly with this patch.

I'm seeing this issue on both x86 Desktop and arm64 Android phone.

On x86 Desktop, this was caused during Ubuntu boot-up. I have a
cronjob installed which calls 'fstrim -v /' during boot. On arm64
Android, this was caused during GC looping with 1ms gc_min_sleep_time
& gc_max_sleep_time."

Root cause of this issue is that f2fs_wait_discard_bios can only be
used by f2fs_put_super, because during put_super there must be no
other referrers, so it can ignore discard entry's reference count
when removing the entry, otherwise in other caller we will hit bug_on
in __remove_discard_cmd as there may be other issuer added reference
count in discard entry.

Thread A				Thread B
					- issue_discard_thread
- f2fs_ioc_fitrim
 - f2fs_trim_fs
  - f2fs_wait_discard_bios
   - __issue_discard_cmd
    - __submit_discard_cmd
					 - __wait_discard_cmd
					  - dc->ref++
					  - __wait_one_discard_bio
   - __wait_discard_cmd
    - __remove_discard_cmd
     - f2fs_bug_on(sbi, dc->ref)

1. Functional Analysis

  - The function rt6_print() is designed to decode and print an IPv6 routing header (type 0 or type 2) from a captured packet.  
  - It takes three parameters:
    • ndo      – a context with printing flags and a pointer ndo->ndo_snapend that marks the end of the available packet data  
    • bp       – a pointer to the start of the routing header in the packet  
    • bp2 (_U_)– unused here  
  - It sets ep = ndo->ndo_snapend to mark the upper bound of safe memory.  
  - It uses ND_TCHECK(dp->ip6r_segleft) to verify that at least the first four bytes of the header (through the segleft field) lie within the captured data.  
  - It reads and prints the header‐length (ip6r_len), routing‐header type, and segleft count.  
  - If the type is 0 or 2, it casts the header to struct ip6_rthdr0, ND_TCHECKs the 32‐bit reserved field, and optionally prints it.  
  - It requires the length field (in eight‐byte units) to be even (each IPv6 address is 16 bytes = two units).  
  - It divides that length by two to get the number of addresses, then loops over them: before printing each address it casts (addr+1) to a byte pointer and checks that it does not exceed ep.  
  - If any check fails, it jumps to a truncation handler that prints “[|srcrt]” and returns –1. Otherwise it closes “)” and returns the header’s total byte length ((len+1)<<3).  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  - Out-of-bounds reads:  
    • Every multi-byte field (segleft, reserved, each IPv6 address) is guarded by either ND_TCHECK or an explicit pointer‐comparison against ep.  
  - Integer arithmetic:  
    • The code uses 8-bit length fields and shifts only after bounds checks; the maximum computed length ((255+1)<<3=2048) is well within reasonable limits, and no wrap-around is possible in 32-bit arithmetic here.  
  - Pointer misuse or undefined behavior:  
    • The loop casts (addr+1) to a u_char* before comparing to ep, so it never compares pointers of different types.  
  - Missing checks:  
    • The code explicitly rejects odd lengths and truncates on any inconsistency.

- Initialization  
  - `pos_x` and `pos_y` track the next pixel’s coordinates in the image (with row 0 at the top).  
  - The destination pixel buffer is zeroed (fully transparent) so any untouched pixels remain transparent.

- Main loop  
  - Continues until we’ve processed all rows (or explicitly hit an “end of bitmap” marker).  
  - Reads two bytes (`buf[0]`, `buf[1]`) from the RLE stream.  
  - If `buf[0] == 0`, this is a control sequence:  
    • `buf[1] == 0`: end of the current scanline → increment `pos_y`, reset `pos_x`.  
    • `buf[1] == 1`: end of the bitmap → break out of the loop.  
    • `buf[1] == 2`: a “delta” → read two more bytes, offset `pos_x` and `pos_y` by those amounts.  
    • otherwise: an uncompressed run of `n_pix = buf[1]` pixels  
       – Compute the padded byte‐count `n_bytes` (padding to a 2-byte boundary).  
       – Read `n_bytes` of palette indices into `buf`.  
       – For each of the `n_pix` indices, look up the RGBA color in the palette and write it into the pixel buffer at `(pos_x, pos_y)`, then advance `pos_x`.

  - If `buf[0] != 0`, this is an RLE‐encoded run:  
    • `n_pix = buf[0]` copies of the same palette index (`buf[1]`), each written as an RGBA pixel, advancing `pos_x` for each.

- Cleanup  
  - On successful completion, returns 1; on any read error or unexpected condition, jumps to `done` and returns 0.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer overflows on `buf`:  
  • Any read length into `buf` is checked (`n_bytes <= sizeof(buf) == 256`).  
  • Uncompressed runs derive `n_bytes` from a single byte and pad to an even boundary; worst‐case `n_bytes` is 256, so reads cannot exceed `buf`.  

- Pixel‐buffer bounds safety:  
  • All writes check `pos_x < width` before writing and increment `pos_x` only inside that check, so `pos_x*4 + bpr*pos_y` cannot exceed the allocated image buffer for valid `pos_x, pos_y`.  
  • Loop exits when `pos_y > height-1`, preventing any out-of-bounds row writes.

- Integer overflow:  
  • `pos_x` and `pos_y` are plain `int`, but they only ever increase up to the image dimensions (or break earlier on end markers). A malicious file could specify many small deltas, but reaching 2^31 would require an implausibly large or infinite file—practically the code either hits the end‐of‐bitmap marker or runs out of input.  

- Infinite‐loop/DoS risk:  
  • A malformed RLE stream that never emits an end‐of‐line or end‐of‐bitmap marker (and keeps `pos_x` below `width` so it never meets the final‐row+end‐of‐line exit condition) could hang or exhaust input until `iwbmp_read` fails. On read failure the code exits, so it does not spin forever in production.  

No unchecked memory writes or arithmetic wrap‐arounds lead to buffer overruns. The code strictly bounds data‐reads and pixel‐writes.

3. Decision

No, the code contains proper bounds checks on its input buffer and on pixel writes and handles read errors gracefully. It does not have a buffer‐overflow or similar vulnerability.

1. Functional Analysis

  - The function MeanShiftImage applies a mean-shift filter to an input image, producing a new image where each pixel is replaced by the average color and location of nearby pixels whose color lies within a specified “color_distance.”
  - It begins by cloning the input image and forcing it into a DirectClass storage representation so that per-pixel reads and writes are efficient.
  - Three “cache views” are acquired:
      • image_view for read-only access to the original image  
      • pixel_view for random read access when probing neighborhood pixels  
      • mean_view for write access to the output (mean) image  
  - An OpenMP parallel loop iterates over each output row y:
      • Fetch pointers p and q to the input and output scanlines.  
      • For each column x:
         1. Initialize a MagickPixelPacket `mean_pixel` from the original pixel at (x,y).  
         2. Initialize `mean_location` to (x,y).  
         3. Repeat up to MaxMeanShiftIterations times:
             – For each offset (u,v) in a roughly circular window of diameter = (width, height):
               • Read the pixel at (round(mean_location.x+u), round(mean_location.y+v)).  
               • If its squared color-distance to the current `mean_pixel` ≤ (color_distance)², accumulate its color and location.  
             – Compute the average color and location (divide by the count of included pixels via PerceptibleReciprocal).  
             – If the shift in combined spatial+color distance from the previous iteration is small (≤ 3.0), break early.  
         4. Clamp the resulting mean_pixel channels back into the Quantum range and write into the output image at (x,y).  
      • Sync the output scanline and update a shared progress counter (with OpenMP atomic) so that a progress monitor can be notified.  
  - After all rows are processed, the cache views are destroyed and the new, filtered image is returned.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  Memory safety  
    - All pixel accesses go through ImageMagick’s cache view APIs (GetCacheViewVirtualPixels, GetOneCacheViewVirtualPixel) which safely handle boundary conditions and guarantee no out-of-bounds memory accesses.  
    - IndexQueue access (indexes+x) is bounded by the row width returned by GetCacheViewVirtualPixels.

  Integer arithmetic  
    - The window loop uses ssize_t for v and u, computed from size_t width/height. If a caller passed extremely large width/height (e.g. > 2·SSIZE_MAX), the cast to ssize_t is formally implementation-defined or undefined. In normal use (modest kernel sizes) this is not an issue.  
    - The code protects against division by zero when averaging by calling PerceptibleReciprocal(count), which returns a safe reciprocal even if count == 0.

  Thread safety  
    - The OpenMP pragma shares `status` and `progress`. The code uses an OpenMP atomic on `progress`. A write to `status` is unprotected, so one thread’s detection of a fatal cache error may not immediately stop other threads—but this would at worst do extra work rather than corrupt memory.  
    - CacheView objects in ImageMagick are designed for per-thread use when driven by magick_number_threads, so the parallel write into disjoint scanlines is safe.

  Denial-of-Service / Performance  
    - A very large width/height or very small color_distance can cause the inner loops to iterate excessively (the window is O(width·height) per pixel, for up to MaxMeanShiftIterations). This is a computational-cost/DoS risk but not a memory corruption vulnerability.

  Summary  
    - No buffer overflows or out-of-bounds reads/writes are introduced.  
    - The code guards against divide-by-zero during averaging, and all memory accesses go through safe ImageMagick APIs.  
    - The only potential risks are unbounded CPU usage with extreme parameters and a minor race on the error flag that would not lead to memory corruption.

3. Decision

  No, the code does not contain memory-safety vulnerabilities or exploitable flaws. It correctly uses the ImageMagick cache API, prevents divide-by-zero, and confines all per-pixel operations within safe bounds.

   This function, `inet_rtnl_recv`, is a callback invoked when there is data to read on a GIOChannel linked to a netlink socket. Roughly, it:

   • Initializes a fixed 4 KiB buffer and a `sockaddr_nl` structure.  
   • Retrieves the underlying file descriptor from the `GIOChannel`.  
   • Calls `recvfrom`, filling the buffer and populating the peer address in `nladdr`.  
   • If `recvfrom` fails with `EINTR` or `EAGAIN`, it returns 0 (no data processed), on other errors –1.  
   • If a zero-length read occurs, returns –1.  
   • Checks `nladdr.nl_pid`; if nonzero, the message is not from the kernel and is ignored (return 0).  
   • Treats the number of bytes read as `len` and walks through the buffer in a loop of nested Netlink messages:  
     – On each iteration it casts `ptr` to `struct nlmsghdr *` (`h`) and uses `NLMSG_OK(h,len)` to ensure the header and claimed length fit in the remaining buffer.  
     – If the message’s sequence number does not match the expected `rth->seq`, it advances `ptr` by `h->nlmsg_len` and decrements `len`, skipping to the next message.  
     – If it encounters `NLMSG_NOOP` or `NLMSG_OVERRUN`, it returns –1.  
     – If it encounters `NLMSG_ERROR`, it extracts the embedded `nlmsgerr`, logs the error text, and returns the negative errno code.  
     – Otherwise it breaks out of the loop with `h` pointing at the matching message.  
   • If `h->nlmsg_seq` equals `rth->seq`, it calls the stored callback with `h`, cancels any timeout, closes and frees the `rtnl` handle.  
   • Returns 0 on normal completion.

1. Functional Analysis

   The function __tipc_sendmsg is responsible for sending a user message over a TIPC socket.  It proceeds roughly through these stages:

   a. Parameter setup and validation  
      - Retrieve internal socket structures (sk, tsk, group, etc.)  
      - Reject messages that exceed TIPC_MAX_USER_MSG_SIZE  
      - If a user address (msg_name) is supplied, validate it and record its addrtype  

   b. Group-socket paths  
      - If the socket is bound to a TIPC group, dispatch to one of several group-send routines (broadcast, anycast, unicast, multicast) based on addrtype  

   c. Peer address resolution (connection-oriented sockets)  
      - If no explicit address was passed, fall back to the socket’s stored peer address  
      - On a connection-oriented (syn) socket, enforce valid state (not LISTEN, already OPEN, not already published), record SYN flag in the header, and possibly record the addrtype for the connection  

   d. Destination lookup for service-range, service-address, or socket-address  
      - Ranges use tipc_sendmcast  
      - Named services use a name table lookup (TIPC_NAMED_MSG path)  
      - Direct socket addresses map straight to a node/ref pair (TIPC_DIRECT_MSG path)  

   e. Congestion blocking  
      - If a known congested link to the destination exists, wait (or bail out on timeout) until the link clears  

   f. Header construction  
      - Fill in destination node/port, message type, header size, name-instance fields (for named messages), etc.  

   g. Payload fragmentation and queueing  
      - Compute the MTU for the destination node  
      - Call tipc_msg_build to fragment the user payload into sk_buffs, enqueuing them on a temporary queue  
      - On SYN messages, clone the sk_buffs into the socket’s sk_write_queue for retransmission  

   h. Transmission  
      - Trace the SKB, then call tipc_node_xmit to actually send them  
      - If the transmit fails with link congestion, mark the link congested for later backoff  
      - On a connection SYN, advance socket state to CONNECTING and wait (up to timeout) for the other side  

   i. Return  
      - On success return dlen; on failure return a negative errno or the number of bytes actually sent  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   - Size checks: dlen is explicitly compared to TIPC_MAX_USER_MSG_SIZE up front. No unbounded copy of user data occurs.  
   - Address validation: tipc_uaddr_valid ensures that msg_name (if supplied) matches the expected structure and length.  
   - Header fields: All msg_set_* calls write into a fixed-size, kernel-controlled header struct; fields are drawn from validated inputs.  
   - Fragmentation: tipc_msg_build creates SKBs sized for the MTU. It returns the actual bytes pushed; mismatch is treated as an error. No overflow.  
   - Queueing and cloning: The code purges and frees packets on failure paths, avoiding leaks.  
   - Concurrency/timing: The send path uses socket timeouts and link-congestion lists, but there is no unchecked loop or race that leads to resource exhaustion.  
   - Error paths consistently return an errno or partial byte count; no NULL dereferences or use-after-free is evident in this linear path.  

   In summary, standard kernel-level checks (length caps, address validation, SKB lifecycle management) are in place. No unchecked pointer arithmetic, no unbounded loops, and no obvious memory corruption or resource leak remain.

3. Decision

   No, the code does not contain any evident vulnerabilities. It performs the necessary size checks, address validation, fragmentation, and error cleanup in a robust manner.

   The function xmlParseMisc(ctxt) scans the input stream pointed to by ctxt and repeatedly consumes any of the following “misc” XML constructs until it reaches end-of-file or a non-misc character:  
   - Processing instructions: when it sees “<?”, it calls xmlParsePI(ctxt) to parse and skip over the entire PI.  
   - Whitespace: when the current character is a blank character (space, tab, newline, etc.), it advances one character (NEXT).  
   - Comments: when it sees “<!--”, it calls xmlParseComment(ctxt) to parse and skip the full comment.  
   The loop exits once none of these patterns match or the parser state indicates EOF.

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - Buffer Overflows: The code uses pointer arithmetic and helper macros (RAW, NXT, CUR_PTR, etc.) but does no unbounded writes; it only advances through existing input. There is no direct buffer write here, so typical overflow issues do not apply.  
   - Out-of-Bounds Reads: The checks (RAW == '<' && NXT(1) == '?') and CMP4 ensure that at least four bytes are available before matching “<!--”. The parser context machinery ordinarily guarantees that NXT(n) is safe to call, so there’s no unchecked read past the buffer.  
   - Infinite Loop / Denial-of-Service: In each branch—PI, whitespace, comment—the code invokes routines or actions that advance the current parsing pointer. Assuming xmlParsePI and xmlParseComment properly consume their entire constructs, the loop will always make forward progress. There is no obvious path that leaves the pointer unadvanced, so it does not hang here.  
   - Injection or Entity Attacks: This snippet only skips whitespace, comments, and PIs; it does not expand entities or process external data by itself. Any external-entity logic would be elsewhere.  

   Overall, this routine simply skips over ignorable content and defers to well-tested helper functions for PIs and comments. There is no evident vulnerability in this focused snippet.

No, the code does not contain a vulnerability in its handling of miscellaneous XML constructs.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `FixSDTPInTRAF` takes a pointer to a `GF_MovieFragmentBox` (moof). If `moof` is NULL, it returns immediately.
- It iterates over each track‐fragment (`traf`) in the movie fragment’s `TrackList`.
- If the track fragment has a `sdtp` box (sample dependency info):
  - It warns if the number of SDTP entries exactly matches the number of track runs (potentially unexpected, but not fatal).
  - It walks through each `trun` (track fragment run) in `traf->TrackRuns`, setting the TRUN flags to enable per‐sample flags and disabling the “first‐sample” shortcut flag.
  - For each sample in the run, it:
    - Checks that the global `sample_index` has not exceeded the number of entries in `sdtp`.
    - Reads the dependency bits (`info`) from `sdtp->sample_info[sample_index]`.
    - Or’s in the corresponding fragment‐dependency flags into the TRUN entry’s `flags`.
    - Increments `sample_index`.
  - If the loop ever finds `sample_index` ≥ `sdtp->sampleCount`, it aborts processing further runs.
  - After processing all runs, if the total processed count doesn’t match `sdtp->sampleCount`, it logs an error.
  - Finally, it removes (`del_parent`) and nulls out the `sdtp` box so it won’t be written out again.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Indexing Safety  
  - The code checks `sample_index < traf->sdtp->sampleCount` before accessing `sample_info[sample_index]`. This prevents an out-of-bounds read of the SDTP array.
- Integer Overflow  
  - `sample_index` and loop counters are 32-bit unsigned. There is no arithmetic that could overflow in a way that leads to mis-indexing.
- Pointer Validity  
  - The function only accesses `traf->sdtp` after confirming it is non-NULL.
  - Removal of `sdtp` at the end is done via the container’s deletion helper; there is no use‐after-free because the local pointer is immediately set to NULL.
- Flag Manipulation  
  - Bitwise OR/AND operations on the `flags` fields are well-defined and cannot corrupt memory.
- Early Abort Path  
  - If the sample counts do not align, the code aborts the loops cleanly and reports an error; it does not proceed to invalid memory.

No unguarded memory accesses, no unchecked integer arithmetic, no buffer overflows or use-after-free scenarios are present in this snippet.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain any vulnerabilities. It includes proper bounds checks and safe manipulation of flags and pointers.
