original_information.commit_message:
mm: thp: fix pmd_bad() triggering in code paths holding mmap_sem read mode

commit 1a5a9906d4e8d1976b701f889d8f35d54b928f25 upstream.

In some cases it may happen that pmd_none_or_clear_bad() is called with
the mmap_sem hold in read mode.  In those cases the huge page faults can
allocate hugepmds under pmd_none_or_clear_bad() and that can trigger a
false positive from pmd_bad() that will not like to see a pmd
materializing as trans huge.

It's not khugepaged causing the problem, khugepaged holds the mmap_sem
in write mode (and all those sites must hold the mmap_sem in read mode
to prevent pagetables to go away from under them, during code review it
seems vm86 mode on 32bit kernels requires that too unless it's
restricted to 1 thread per process or UP builds).  The race is only with
the huge pagefaults that can convert a pmd_none() into a
pmd_trans_huge().

Effectively all these pmd_none_or_clear_bad() sites running with
mmap_sem in read mode are somewhat speculative with the page faults, and
the result is always undefined when they run simultaneously.  This is
probably why it wasn't common to run into this.  For example if the
madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) runs zap_page_range() shortly before the page
fault, the hugepage will not be zapped, if the page fault runs first it
will be zapped.

Altering pmd_bad() not to error out if it finds hugepmds won't be enough
to fix this, because zap_pmd_range would then proceed to call
zap_pte_range (which would be incorrect if the pmd become a
pmd_trans_huge()).

The simplest way to fix this is to read the pmd in the local stack
(regardless of what we read, no need of actual CPU barriers, only
compiler barrier needed), and be sure it is not changing under the code
that computes its value.  Even if the real pmd is changing under the
value we hold on the stack, we don't care.  If we actually end up in
zap_pte_range it means the pmd was not none already and it was not huge,
and it can't become huge from under us (khugepaged locking explained
above).

All we need is to enforce that there is no way anymore that in a code
path like below, pmd_trans_huge can be false, but pmd_none_or_clear_bad
can run into a hugepmd.  The overhead of a barrier() is just a compiler
tweak and should not be measurable (I only added it for THP builds).  I
don't exclude different compiler versions may have prevented the race
too by caching the value of *pmd on the stack (that hasn't been
verified, but it wouldn't be impossible considering
pmd_none_or_clear_bad, pmd_bad, pmd_trans_huge, pmd_none are all inlines
and there's no external function called in between pmd_trans_huge and
pmd_none_or_clear_bad).

		if (pmd_trans_huge(*pmd)) {
			if (next-addr != HPAGE_PMD_SIZE) {
				VM_BUG_ON(!rwsem_is_locked(&tlb->mm->mmap_sem));
				split_huge_page_pmd(vma->vm_mm, pmd);
			} else if (zap_huge_pmd(tlb, vma, pmd, addr))
				continue;
			/* fall through */
		}
		if (pmd_none_or_clear_bad(pmd))

Because this race condition could be exercised without special
privileges this was reported in CVE-2012-1179.

The race was identified and fully explained by Ulrich who debugged it.
I'm quoting his accurate explanation below, for reference.

    following is logged on the console:

      mm/memory.c:145: bad pmd ffff8800376e1f98(80000000314000e7).

    The "bad pmd ..." message is logged by pmd_clear_bad() before it clears
    the page's PMD table entry.

        handle_mm_fault

    The mmap_sem does not prevent the race because both threads are acquiring
    it in shared mode (down_read).  Thread B holds the page_table_lock while

1. Functional Analysis

- Early VM86 Mode Handling  
  If the VM flag (EFLAGS.VM) is set, the code fabricates a real-mode–style segment descriptor:  
  • `base = sel << 4`, `limit = 0xFFFF`, `attr.bytes = 0xF3`  
  • Stores it via `hvm_set_segment_register()` and returns success.

- NULL Selector Check  
  If the selector’s index bits are zero (`sel & 0xFFFC == 0`):  
  • CS or SS with NULL selector is illegal → jump to failure.  
  • Otherwise, zero out the segment register and return success.

- LDT/GDT Table Selection & Presence  
  • For LDTR loads, ensures the TI bit is clear (must reference GDT).  
  • Fetches the current CS register and the descriptor table (GDT or LDT) register.  
  • Verifies the descriptor table’s Present bit (P) and that the selector index lies within the table limit.

- Descriptor Fetch & Caching  
  • Maps the descriptor entry from guest memory with `hvm_map_entry()`.  
  • Copies it locally into `desc`.

- Type & Privilege Checks  
  • Verifies the descriptor’s “system vs. code/data” bit matches the requested segment (e.g. you can’t load a data descriptor into CS).  
  • Extracts DPL (descriptor privilege), RPL (selector privilege), and CPL (current privilege).  
  • For each segment kind (CS, SS, LDTR, other DS/ES/FS/GS), enforces the Intel-defined checks:  
    – CS: must be code, conforming rules if EC=0, DPL/RPL constraints.  
    – SS: must be writable data, DPL==CPL==RPL.  
    – LDTR: must be system LDT descriptor.  
    – Others: data or readable code, DPL vs. CPL/RPL rules for data vs. non-conforming code.  
  • Checks the Present bit; on SS fault_type switches to stack fault if not present.

- Accessed Bit Setting Loop  
  • If the Accessed bit isn’t already set in the descriptor, attempts a cmpxchg to set it in guest memory (if the mapping is writable).  
  • Retries until either it succeeds in setting the bit or it discovers the bit is already set.

- Register Update  
  • Unmaps the descriptor entry.  
  • Constructs the segment base, limit, and attributes from the raw descriptor fields (handling G=true granularity).  
  • Stores the selector in the register and calls `hvm_set_segment_register()` to update the VCPU’s segment register.  
  • Returns success.

- Error Paths  
  • On any check failure, unmaps the descriptor if needed, injects a hardware exception with the appropriate trap number and selector, and returns failure.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Bounds Checking  
  • The code verifies the selector’s index against the descriptor table limit before mapping.  
  • It checks P (present) in both the descriptor table and the descriptor itself.

- Privilege & Type Enforcement  
  • All Intel-required S-bit, code/data, conforming/non-conforming, DPL/RPL/CPL, and writable checks are present and correctly branched based on the segment being loaded.

- Race Conditions / TOCTOU  
  • The only potentially racy operation is setting the Accessed bit via cmpxchg, but this loop correctly handles concurrent updates and does not rely on stale values for privilege checks:  
    – Privilege and type checks are done before attempting to set the Accessed bit.  
    – Once the checks pass, setting the Accessed bit cannot change the segment’s protection semantics.

- Integer Overflows  
  • Selector arithmetic `(sel & 0xFFF8) + 7` is on unsigned and compared against an unsigned 32-bit limit; no overflow is possible for a 16-bit selector.  
  • Base and limit recomposition use well-defined bit masks and shifts.

- Memory Safety  
  • The only direct memory access is via `hvm_map_entry()`, which returns NULL on failure. The code handles that.  
  • The local copy of the descriptor prevents use-after-unmap.

Overall, each architectural check mandated by the Intel/AMD manuals is present, and all resource limits and edge cases are handled or faulted appropriately.

3. Decision

No, the code correctly enforces all segment validation rules and contains no obvious vulnerabilities. It handles errors, privilege checks, boundary checks, and concurrent Accessed-bit updates safely.

1. Functional Analysis

The function vgic_v2_distr_mmio_read emulates reads by a guest VM from the GIC Distributor’s MMIO region. Its high-level structure is:

 • Compute the register offset  
   – gicd_reg = guest physical address minus the VGIC distributor base.  
 • Select the guest register (dabt.reg) in which to place the result.  
 • Increment a performance counter for GICD reads.  
 • Switch on gicd_reg:  
   – For each defined GICD register (e.g. CTLR, TYPER, IIDR, IGROUPR, ISENABLER, etc.),  
     • Verify the access size (DABT_BYTE or DABT_WORD) and sign-extension as needed.  
     • Map the offset to an internal data structure (vgic_irq_rank) via vgic_rank_offset().  
     • Acquire either the global distributor lock (vgic_lock) or a per-rank lock (vgic_lock_rank).  
     • Read the appropriate field (ienable, ipend, iactive, itargets, ipriority, icfg, etc.)  
     • Release the lock  
     • Write the value into the selected guest register and return “handled”.  
   – For ranges explicitly defined as “read-as-zero” or unimplemented, it zeroes or returns a dummy value.  
   – For unsupported widths, it prints an error and crashes the guest domain.  
   – For completely unknown offsets, it logs an error and returns “not handled.”  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

 • Bounds/oob indexing  
   – gicd_reg is derived by subtraction; negative or excessively large values fall through to the default case and are not used to index any array.  
   – All rank-array accesses go through vgic_rank_offset(), which returns NULL if the index would be out of range. Those paths jump to “read_as_zero” rather than dereferencing invalid memory.  

 • Access-size validation  
   – Every case checks dabt.size against allowed sizes and rejects (crashes the guest) on a bad width, preventing misaligned or partial reads from indexing arrays incorrectly.  

 • Concurrency/races  
   – Shared data are protected by either the global VGICD lock or per-rank spinlocks around every read of the in-memory state.  

 • Denial-of-service  
   – A malicious guest could intentionally use bad sizes or illegal offsets to force repeated domain_crash_synchronous() calls (i.e. crash itself), but it cannot crash the hypervisor or other tenants.

   – The code never exposes data from one guest to another or from the hypervisor itself. Unimplemented or secure-world bits read back as zero or a fixed dummy.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function dbFree(ip, blkno, nblocks) is responsible for freeing a sequence of data blocks in JFS’s block‐allocation bitmap (“dmap”).
- It begins by taking a shared (read) lock on the on‐disk dmap inode to serialize metadata updates.
- It checks that blkno is nonzero and that blkno + nblocks does not exceed the total number of blocks managed by the bitmap.  If the range is out of bounds, it logs an error and returns –EIO.
- If the filesystem was mounted with discard (TRIM) support and the range is at least the minimum discard size, it issues a discard request for that range.
- It then walks the range one dmap page at a time:
  • If there was a previously held metapage, it writes it back out  
  • It computes the dmap page number using BLKTODMAP, reads that page into memory (metapage)  
  • It computes how many blocks in the current dmap page can be freed (nb = min(remaining, blocks until dmap boundary))  
  • It calls dbFreeDmap to clear those bits in the dmap page; on error it cleans up and returns the error code  
- After the loop, it writes out the final metapage (if any), releases the lock, and returns success (0).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Bounds checking: The code rejects blkno==0 and any (blkno + nblocks) past the total map size.  That prevents out‐of‐bounds writes into the bitmap.
- Integer overflow: blkno and nblocks are 64‐bit signed.  A maliciously negative nblocks could underflow the (blkno + nblocks) check, but blkno is unsigned (cast from s64) and negative nblocks would make (blkno+nblocks) < blkno so pass the bounds check, yet the rem > 0 loop guard fails immediately and nothing is freed.  No memory corruption can occur.
- Metapage accesses: Every read_metapage is balanced by a write_metapage or release_metapage on error; there is no unchecked indexing into mp->data.
- Locking: The shared lock prevents concurrent dmap writers; calling write_metapage under a read lock is unconventional but does not introduce a consistency or security hole here.
- Other attacks (race, use‐after‐free, double‐free) are mitigated by the linear walk and single‐threaded update under lock.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a vulnerability: it performs proper range checks, manages its metapages and locking correctly, and contains no unchecked memory or arithmetic operations that lead to corruption.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `add_ballooned_pages(int nr_pages)` attempts to allocate or “balloon” a specified number of pages into the system’s free page pool.
- At the top, it checks a Xen-specific flag `xen_hotplug_unpopulated`. If hotplug space is unpopulated:
  - It calls `reserve_additional_memory()`, which may initiate a memory reservation or return a state code.
  - If the reservation did **not** return `BP_ECANCELED`, it:
    - Releases the global `balloon_mutex`.
    - Sleeps on `balloon_wq` until the list `ballooned_pages` is non-empty.
    - Reacquires `balloon_mutex` and returns success (0).
- If hotplug is populated (or the reservation was canceled), it checks whether at least `nr_pages` are available via `si_mem_available()`. If not, it returns `-ENOMEM`.
- It then attempts to “decrease” a memory reservation by calling `decrease_reservation(nr_pages, GFP_USER)`. If that does not return `BP_DONE`, it returns `-ENOMEM`; otherwise it returns success (0).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- There is no user-supplied pointer arithmetic or buffer manipulation, so there is no risk of buffer overflow or out-of-bounds memory access.
- The code correctly checks return codes from both `reserve_additional_memory()` and `decrease_reservation()`, and returns error codes on failure.
- The use of `wait_event()` with the mutex properly unlocked before sleeping and relocked after wakeup avoids deadlock. The sleep/wake is bounded by list non-emptiness and will wake up only when pages are actually ballooned.
- The check of `si_mem_available()` followed by a reservation attempt is subject to normal race conditions on available memory, but the function handles insufficient memory by returning `-ENOMEM`. This is the expected behavior in a concurrent kernel environment and not a security issue.
- No other synchronization mistakes or unchecked pointers are evident.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain a vulnerability. It performs proper state checks, error handling, and synchronization.

A use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's af_unix component can be exploited to achieve local privilege escalation.

The unix_stream_sendpage() function tries to add data to the last skb in the peer's recv queue without locking the queue. Thus there is a race where unix_stream_sendpage() could access an skb locklessly that is being released by garbage collection, resulting in use-after-free.

original_information.commit_msg:
Bing-Jhong Billy Jheng reported null-ptr-deref in unix_stream_sendpage()
with detailed analysis and a nice repro.

unix_stream_sendpage() tries to add data to the last skb in the peer's
recv queue without locking the queue.

If the peer's FD is passed to another socket and the socket's FD is
passed to the peer, there is a loop between them.  If we close both
sockets without receiving FD, the sockets will be cleaned up by garbage
collection.

The garbage collection iterates such sockets and unlinks skb with
FD from the socket's receive queue under the queue's lock.

So, there is a race where unix_stream_sendpage() could access an skb
locklessly that is being released by garbage collection, resulting in
use-after-free.

To avoid the issue, unix_stream_sendpage() must lock the peer's recv
queue.

Note the issue does not exist in 6.5+ thanks to the recent sendpage()
refactoring.

This patch is originally written by Linus Torvalds.

  - Runs a primality test on q, flagging `DH_CHECK_Q_NOT_PRIME` if composite.
  - Checks that q divides p−1 exactly, else flags `DH_CHECK_INVALID_Q_VALUE`.

original_information.cve_description:
Issue summary: Checking excessively long DH keys or parameters may be very slow.

Impact summary: Applications that use the functions DH_check(), DH_check_ex()
or EVP_PKEY_param_check() to check a DH key or DH parameters may experience long
delays. Where the key or parameters that are being checked have been obtained
from an untrusted source this may lead to a Denial of Service.

The function DH_check() performs various checks on DH parameters. After fixing
CVE-2023-3446 it was discovered that a large q parameter value can also trigger
an overly long computation during some of these checks. A correct q value,
if present, cannot be larger than the modulus p parameter, thus it is
unnecessary to perform these checks if q is larger than p.

An application that calls DH_check() and supplies a key or parameters obtained
from an untrusted source could be vulnerable to a Denial of Service attack.

The function DH_check() is itself called by a number of other OpenSSL functions.
An application calling any of those other functions may similarly be affected.
The other functions affected by this are DH_check_ex() and
EVP_PKEY_param_check().

Also vulnerable are the OpenSSL dhparam and pkeyparam command line applications
when using the "-check" option.

The OpenSSL SSL/TLS implementation is not affected by this issue.

The OpenSSL 3.0 and 3.1 FIPS providers are not affected by this issue.

DH_check(): Do not try checking q properties if it is obviously invalid

q is not large either when performing subsequent tests using that

computations.

1.1 File-based PAC retrieval  
  - If the URL scheme is “file” or “pac+file”, the code opens the local file (m_path) for reading.  
  - It uses fstat to get the file size, enforces a maximum allowed size (PAC_MAX_SIZE), allocates a buffer of size st_size+1 (zero-initialized), reads the entire file into that buffer, and returns it (with a terminating NUL).  

1.2 DNS lookup and TCP connect  
  - For non-file schemes the code calls get_ips(true) to resolve m_host into a list of IPv4/IPv6 addresses.  
  - It iterates through each returned sockaddr, creates a SOCK_STREAM socket, and attempts connect(…) until one succeeds.  

1.3 HTTP request construction and send  
  - It builds an HTTP/1.1 GET request line using m_path (or “/” if empty) plus m_query, then adds standard headers: Host, Accept (PAC_MIME_TYPE), Connection: close, and a blank line.  
  - It calls send(…) to write the entire request.  

1.4 HTTP response parsing  
  - It reads the status line via recvline(…) and sscanf’s out the response code; it proceeds only on “HTTP/1.x 200”.  
  - It then reads headers line-by-line until the blank line, checking for “Transfer-Encoding: chunked” (or legacy Content-Transfer-Encoding) and parsing a “Content-Length: <N>” if present.  

1.5 Body download (supporting chunked or content-length)  
  - If chunked mode is detected, it loops: read a chunk-size line (hex), break on a zero chunk or parse failure, add that size to content_length, then read exactly that many bytes (or up to PAC_MAX_SIZE).  
  - If not chunked, it reads until either Content-Length bytes are received or the connection closes.  
  - All data is accumulated in a std::vector<char> dynamic_buffer. If the total would exceed PAC_MAX_SIZE at any point, it aborts and clears the buffer.  

1.6 Finalization  
  - If the downloaded size matches the declared content_length (or if no content_length was declared but data arrived), it allocates a NUL-terminated char* buffer, memcpy’s the data in, and returns it.  
  - In all cases it cleanly shuts down and closes the socket before returning.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

2.1 Buffer overflow / heap overflow  
  - The code uses std::vector<char> for incremental reads, resizing only by the exact amount requested, and caps at PAC_MAX_SIZE.  
  - When copying into a final char* it allocates exactly (size+1) bytes and appends a NUL. No out-of-bounds writes are evident.  

2.2 Integer overflow  
  - content_length is an unsigned long; chunk sizes are read into an unsigned int. A maliciously large chunk-length line could wrap content_length, but the subsequent logic will see content_length < PAC_MAX_SIZE and only read that (wrapped) amount. It cannot exceed the vector’s bounds.  

2.3 Partial reads / error returns  
  - recv() return ≤ 0 or growing beyond PAC_MAX_SIZE causes an immediate break and clearing of dynamic_buffer. Incomplete or error reads do not leave the code writing past the end of the buffer.  
  - In the file branch, read() errors (return < 0) are not distinguished from a short read >0; a negative return will leave buffer untouched but zero-initialized. No overflow, but possibly erroneous empty data.  

2.4 HTTP header injection / request smuggling  
  - The GET line is built by concatenating m_path and m_query directly into the request without stripping or percent-encoding CRLF. If m_path or m_query contains embedded “\r” or “\n”, an attacker controlling the URL object could inject spurious headers or a faulty request line. This can lead to request-smuggling or header-injection attacks.  

2.5 Incomplete MIME-type check  
  - The code sends an “Accept: application/x-ns-proxy-autoconfig” header but never verifies a “Content-Type” response header. It will happily download arbitrary content and hand it off for PAC evaluation. This is more a logic oversight than a memory corruption.  

2.6 Resource cleanup  
  - On every error path the socket is properly closed (close or closesocket) and in the file case the file descriptor is closed. No obvious file or socket descriptor leak is present.  

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain buffer-overflow or memory-safety vulnerabilities. It does allow HTTP header injection if m_path/m_query can include CRLF, and it does not verify the returned Content-Type, but it carefully bounds all heap allocations and prevents out-of-bounds writes.

original_information.commit_msg:
gvariant: Don’t allow child elements to overlap with each other

If different elements of a variable sized array can overlap with each
other then we can cause a `GVariant` to normalise to a much larger type.

This commit changes the behaviour of `GVariant` with non-normal form data. If
an invalid frame offset is found all subsequent elements are given their
default value.

When retrieving an element at index `n` we scan the frame offsets up to index
`n` and if they are not in order we return an element with the default value
for that type.  This guarantees that elements don't overlap with each
other.  We remember the offset we've scanned up to so we don't need to
repeat this work on subsequent accesses.  We skip these checks for trusted
data.

Unfortunately this makes random access of untrusted data O(n) — at least
on first access.  It doesn't affect the algorithmic complexity of accessing
elements in order, such as when using the `GVariantIter` interface.  Also:
the cost of validation will be amortised as the `GVariant` instance is
continued to be used.

I've implemented this with 4 different functions, 1 for each element size,
rather than looping calling `gvs_read_unaligned_le` in the hope that the
compiler will find it easy to optimise and should produce fairly tight
code.

Fixes: #2121

the `-policy' argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `CopyRectangle(rfbClient* client, uint8_t* buffer, int x, int y, int w, int h)` is intended to copy a rectangular block of pixel data from the source `buffer` into the client’s in-memory frame buffer.
- It first checks whether `client->frameBuffer` is non-NULL; if NULL it returns immediately.
- It then calls `CheckRect(client, x, y, w, h)` to verify that the requested rectangle (top-left corner `(x,y)`, width `w`, height `h`) lies entirely within the dimensions of the client’s frame buffer. If this check fails, it logs a “Rect out of bounds” message and returns.
- A macro `COPY_RECT(BPP)` is defined to handle the actual copying for a given bits-per-pixel (`BPP`). Inside the macro:
  - `rs` is calculated as the number of bytes in each row of the source rectangle: `rs = w * (BPP/8)`.
  - `rs2` is the number of bytes per full frame-buffer row: `rs2 = client->width * (BPP/8)`.
  - A loop variable `j` is initialized to the byte offset in the frame buffer for pixel `(x,y)`, i.e.  
      `j = x*(BPP/8) + y*rs2`.  
    The loop iterates one frame-buffer row at a time, for `h` rows total (`j < (y+h)*rs2`), incrementing `j` by `rs2` on each pass.
  - On each iteration, `memcpy` copies `rs` bytes from `buffer` into `client->frameBuffer + j`, then advances `buffer` by `rs` to point to the next source row.
- Finally, a `switch` on `client->format.bitsPerPixel` selects `COPY_RECT(8)`, `COPY_RECT(16)`, or `COPY_RECT(32)` for 8-, 16-, or 32-bit pixel formats respectively. Any other bit depth is reported as unsupported.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Bounds checking:  
  The call to `CheckRect` (presumably) ensures `0 ≤ x < client->width`, `0 ≤ y < client->height`, and `x+w ≤ client->width`, `y+h ≤ client->height`. As long as `CheckRect` is correctly implemented, the computed byte offsets `j` and the copy lengths `rs` will never exceed the allocated frame-buffer size. Thus there is no out-of-bounds write to the frame buffer.
- Integer overflow:  
  The intermediate multiplications (`w * (BPP/8)` and `client->width * (BPP/8)`) occur in 32-bit `int`. In theory, if `w` or `client->width` were large enough, these products could overflow and wrap around, defeating the bounds checks. In practice, pixel dimensions are negotiated to reasonable display sizes (e.g. thousands of pixels, not millions) so overflow is highly unlikely. If one wanted to be extra cautious, those computations could be promoted to 64-bit or range-checked.
- Source-buffer length:  
  The function assumes that `buffer` points to at least `w*h*(bitsPerPixel/8)` bytes of valid data. There is no explicit length check here, so if an upstream caller passed a shorter buffer, a read-past-end of `buffer` could occur. However, in typical usage of the RFB library, the network-message parser enforces the exact rectangle payload size before calling `CopyRectangle`.
- Unsupported bit depths:  
  If `bitsPerPixel` is not 8, 16, or 32, the code merely logs an “Unsupported bitsPerPixel” message and does not attempt a copy. There is no risk of accidental misuse in that case.

3. Decision

No, the code as written does not contain a direct vulnerability. It relies on a correct implementation of `CheckRect` and an upstream guarantee of buffer length, but within this function there is no unchecked memory write or overflow.

- The function exif_process_APP12 takes an ImageInfo pointer, a buffer, and its length.  
- It skips the first two bytes of the buffer (presumably header/identifier bytes) and computes l1 = the length of the first zero‐terminated string, up to a maximum of (length − 2) bytes, via php_strnlen(buffer+2, length−2).  
- If l1 > 0, it adds a “Company” tag whose value is the first string (buffer+2, length l1).  
- It then checks whether there remain more bytes beyond that first string plus its terminator (i.e. length > 2 + l1 + 1).  
- If so, it computes l2 the same way starting at buffer+2+l1+1, and adds an “Info” tag of length l2 at that offset.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer overflows / over-reads: For a well‐formed JPEG APP12 segment, length is always ≥2 (the segment length includes the two length‐bytes themselves).  
  - When length ≥ 2, the call php_strnlen(buffer+2, length−2) will never read past buffer+length, so l1 is correctly bounded.  
  - The second string is only queried if length > 2 + l1 + 1, so that region also stays in‐bounds.  
- Integer underflow: If length < 2, then length−2 underflows size_t, leading to a huge length argument to php_strnlen and a potential out-of-bounds read.  
  - However, by the JPEG/EXIF specification an APP12 segment must encode a 16-bit length ≥2, so in normal use length<2 should not occur.  
- Null‐termination: php_strnlen enforces a maximum, so if the buffer contains no zero byte within the permitted range, it will stop at the bound rather than scanning indefinitely.  
- Conclusion: under the specification’s guaranteed segment size (length ≥2), there are no out-of-bounds reads or other exploitable conditions. Only a grossly malformed length<2 (which shouldn’t appear in valid EXIF data) could trigger an issue—which is outside normal operation.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain exploitable vulnerabilities under normal EXIF APP12 segment constraints.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function ext4_init_block_bitmap initializes the block bitmap for a given block group in an ext4 filesystem.
- It takes a superblock pointer (sb), a locked buffer_head (bh) that will hold the bitmap, the block_group index, and a pointer to the group descriptor (gdp).
- First it verifies the descriptor checksum; if that fails it marks the group as corrupted and returns -EFSBADCRC.
- It zeroes out the entire bitmap buffer (memset).
- It computes bit_max, the number of metadata clusters in the group, and checks that bit_max bits will fit in the buffer (bit_max>>3 < buffer size); if not, it returns –EFSCORRUPTED.
- It sets all bits [0, bit_max) to 1 (marking them “used” initially).
- It computes the absolute block number of the first data block in the group.
- It locates the block bitmap block, inode bitmap block, and inode table blocks, and for each one that lies within this group, it computes its relative cluster index and sets that bit in the bitmap.
- Finally, it marks any bits from the actual number of clusters in the group up to the full bitmap size as “used” (ending region), then returns success (0).

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Buffer overflow: before setting bits, the code checks that (bit_max >> 3) is strictly less than bh->b_size. Since bit_max is the number of bits to set and bh->b_size is in bytes, this guarantees the bitmap writes stay within the b_data buffer. No out-of-bounds is possible in the bit-setting loops.
- Integer overflow: bit_max and bh->b_size are unsigned, and the shift‐and‐compare pattern preserves correct range checks without wraparound.
- Use-after-free or uninitialized memory: buffer_head is assumed locked and valid; the code explicitly zeroes it before use.
- Descriptor integrity: a bad checksum aborts initialization rather than proceeding with corrupted metadata.
- No user‐supplied arithmetic (no path for attacker‐controlled overflow).
- All loops iterate over bounded counts derived from filesystem metadata; no unbounded recursion or syscall.

3. Decision

No. The code correctly bounds all writes, validates metadata checksums, and contains no exploitable buffer overflows or arithmetic flaws.

   The function `vhost_vdpa_config_put` takes a pointer `v` to a `struct vhost_vdpa`. Inside the function:  
   - It checks whether `v->config_ctx` is non-NULL.  
   - If it is, it calls `eventfd_ctx_put(v->config_ctx)`, which typically decrements the reference count on that eventfd context (and may free it if the count reaches zero).  
   - After calling `eventfd_ctx_put`, it sets `v->config_ctx` to NULL to mark that the context has been released and prevent any further accidental reuse.

   • Use‐after‐free: After the first call, `v->config_ctx` is NULL’d, so subsequent users of `v->config_ctx` would see NULL rather than a dangling pointer. That prevents a straightforward use‐after‐free via this member.  
   • NULL‐dereference: The code checks for NULL before dereferencing `v->config_ctx`, so it can never deference a NULL pointer here.  
   • Concurrency/race conditions: If two threads attempt to call `vhost_vdpa_config_put` concurrently on the same `v`, one will do the `eventfd_ctx_put` and NULL the pointer, and the other will see it as NULL and skip it. There is no direct memory corruption, although higher‐level synchronization might still be required if multiple threads can touch `v->config_ctx` at once.  
   In summary, this snippet safely releases a resource exactly once and zeroes its pointer. There is no obvious vulnerability in this isolated piece of code.

3. Decision  
   No, this code is not vulnerable. It correctly checks for NULL, prevents double‐free by NULL’ing the pointer after release, and avoids use‐after‐free or NULL‐dereference in its own logic.

   The function ossl_policy_cache_set_mapping takes an X509 certificate `x` and a stack of POLICY_MAPPING structures `maps`. Its goal is to integrate a set of policy mappings into the certificate’s existing policy cache. In detail:

   • It retrieves the certificate’s policy cache via `x->policy_cache`.  
   • If `maps` is empty, it records an error (`ret = -1`) and jumps to cleanup.  
   • For each POLICY_MAPPING in `maps`:  
     – It rejects mappings that involve the special anyPolicy OID on either side.  
     – It looks up existing policy data for the issuerDomainPolicy in the cache.  
     – If none is found and the cache contains an anyPolicy entry, it clones that anyPolicy data (sharing its qualifier set) and marks it as a mapped-any entry, then pushes it into the cache.  
     – If policy data already exists, it simply marks that entry as “mapped.”  
     – It appends the subjectDomainPolicy OID to the policy data’s expected‐policy set. In successful cases, it steals the raw ASN1_OBJECT pointer by nulling out the mapping’s field.  
   • After processing all entries, it sets `ret = 1` to indicate success.  
   • In every case (success or error) it frees the POLICY_MAPPING stack via `sk_POLICY_MAPPING_pop_free`.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   • Out-of-bounds or buffer overflow: No manual buffer or string operations are done; only ASN1_OBJECT pointers are moved among internal stacks. The code always checks push results and bails out on failure.  
   • Null dereference: The code assumes `x->policy_cache` is non-NULL but that is a precondition of the caller. All subsequent pointer uses are guarded by checks.  
   • Memory leaks / double frees:  
     – On success or error, the POLICY_MAPPING stack is freed exactly once.  
     – Any ASN1_OBJECT stolen from a mapping is removed from the mapping struct before its free and added to the cache’s stacks exactly once.  
     – There is no path that loses ownership without freeing or that frees the same pointer twice.  
   • Policy logic bypass: The function rejects mappings that refer to anyPolicy and only creates new entries if an anyPolicy slot already existed, in accordance with RFC rules.  
   • Denial-of-service via large stacks: This is a generic resource-exhaustion risk (large alloc requests), but the code checks each allocation result and fails safely rather than corrupting memory.

   In sum, the function performs the intended transformations, validates inputs, checks error returns, and manages ownership correctly. No memory safety or logic-bypass vulnerabilities are evident.

3. Decision

   No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities. It properly validates, allocates, and frees all resources, and enforces policy-mapping constraints.

original_information.cve_description:
If an X.509 certificate contains a malformed policy constraint and
policy processing is enabled, then a write lock will be taken twice
recursively.  On some operating systems (most widely: Windows) this
results in a denial of service when the affected process hangs.  Policy
processing being enabled on a publicly facing server is not considered
to be a common setup.

Policy processing is enabled by passing the `-policy'
argument to the command line utilities or by calling the
`X509_VERIFY_PARAM_set1_policies()' function.

Update (31 March 2023): The description of the policy processing enablement
was corrected based on CVE-2023-0466.

     – Checks that bb, in, and out pointers are non-NULL.  
     – Extracts the AES key schedule (state->erk) and number of rounds from the AESNI_State.  
     – Rejects an illegal round‐count (>14).  
     – Loads the expanded round keys into a local __m128i array r[0..rounds].  
   
   • Main “8‐block” encryption loop  
     – While at least 8 blocks (8×16=128 bytes) remain:  
       • Load 8 plaintext blocks with unaligned loads (_mm_loadu_si128).  
       • XOR each block with the first round key (r[0]).  
       • Perform the first 9 rounds of AESENC in one loop (j=1..9).  
       • If the key schedule has more rounds (e.g. for AES‐192 or AES‐256), run the extra rounds: j=10..rounds–1.  
       • Execute the final round with _mm_aesenclast_si128(data[i], r[rounds]).  
       • Store all 8 ciphertext blocks back with unaligned stores (_mm_storeu_si128).  
   
   • Tail “up to 7 blocks” encryption loop  
     – For each remaining full 16‐byte block:  
       • Load one block, XOR with r[0].  
       • Perform rounds 1..9 via a simple for‐loop.  
       • If rounds>10, perform the extra rounds by stepping i in pairs (i=10,12, …).  
       • Finalize with _mm_aesenclast_si128 and store the result.  
   
   • Leftover check  
     – If any bytes remain (data_len>0 but <16), return ERR_NOT_ENOUGH_DATA.  
     – Otherwise, return 0 to indicate success.

   – Memory safety:  
     • All loads/stores occur only when data_len guarantees enough bytes.  
     • The local round‐key array r is sized to hold up to 15 keys (14 rounds + initial), matching the max of AES‐256.  
   – Key schedule bounds:  
     • The code rejects “rounds” values >14.  
     • For standard AES key sizes (10, 12, 14 rounds), the loops cover exactly the right number of rounds.  
   – Side‐channel resistance:  
     • Uses AES‐NI instructions (constant‐time, no secret‐dependent table lookups).  
   – Error handling:  
     • Partial‐block trailing data triggers an error return, and no out‐of‐bounds memory access occurs.  

   No buffer overflows, no secret‐dependent memory access patterns, no use‐after‐free or NULL dereference beyond the initial checks.  

3. Decision  
   
   No, the code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities; it correctly bounds inputs, handles AES‐NI rounds safely, and avoids side‐channel leaks.

1. Functional Analysis

The function xfs_swapext takes a pointer to an xfs_swapext_t structure (sxp), which encodes two user-supplied file descriptors and an extent‐swapping request. Its steps are:

  • fget the “target” descriptor sx_fdtarget into file  
    – If fget fails, return EINVAL  
    – Verify file is open for read and write and that O_APPEND was not set; if not, return EBADF  

  • fget the “temporary” descriptor sx_fdtmp into tmp_file  
    – If fget fails, return EINVAL  
    – Verify tmp_file is open for read and write and that O_APPEND was not set; if not, return EBADF  

  • Check neither underlying inode is marked as a swapfile  
    – If either is a swapfile, return EINVAL  

  • Convert file->f_path.dentry->d_inode and tmp_file->... to XFS inodes (ip and tip)  
  • Ensure both inodes live on the same XFS mount and are not the same inode; if either check fails, return EINVAL  
  • Check the XFS filesystem is not in forced shutdown; if it is, return EIO  

  • Call the core routine xfs_swap_extents(ip, tip, sxp) to perform the swap  
  • fput the tmp_file and file structs before returning the final error code  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  a) File‐mode/time‐of‐check time‐of‐use  
     • The code fetches the file struct via fget(), checks its f_mode and f_flags, then later invokes xfs_swap_extents() without re‐checking those flags. A racing thread could fcntl(… , F_SETFL, O_APPEND) on the same fd between the check and the swap call. The code does not lock the file flags to prevent that TOCTOU.  
     – Impact: Depending on xfs_swap_extents()’s behavior under O_APPEND, the swap could inadvertently append blocks or corrupt data ordering.  

  b) No explicit regular‐file check  
     • The code allows any open file with read/write, not just S_IFREG. Special devices or sockets opened RDWR could be passed in.  
     – Impact: Casting a non‐XFS inode to an XFS inode (via XFS_I()) can lead to type confusion or crashes if the underlying sb/inode layout is not XFS.  

  c) No mount‐type verification  
     • The function only tests that both inodes share the same ip->i_mount, not that this is an XFS superblock. If one or both fds refer to files on a non‐XFS filesystem exported into this syscall path, XFS_I() will misinterpret the inode structure.  
     – Impact: Kernel panic or memory corruption when accessing XFS‐specific fields on a non‐XFS inode.  

  d) Swapfile detection and same‐inode guard  
     • These checks guard against trivial misuse (swapping a swapfile or swapping a file-range with itself), which is correct.  

  e) Forced‐shutdown check  
     • Properly aborts if the filesystem is read‐only or has been shut down.  

3. Decision

No, the code is not fully safe. It fails to lock file flags against concurrent mode changes (TOCTOU), does not verify that inodes are regular XFS files, and will miscast non‐XFS inodes via XFS_I(), potentially crashing the kernel.

a write-only file owned by user "bar" into a file owned by "foo" and

1. Functional Analysis

  - The function `_gdContributionsAlloc` takes two unsigned ints, `line_length` and `windows_size`.  
  - It first checks for overflow when computing the total byte‐size of a weight array (`windows_size × sizeof(double)`). If that check fails, it returns NULL.  
  - It allocates a `LineContribType` struct (`res`) and stores `windows_size` and `line_length` in it.  
  - It checks for overflow when computing `line_length × sizeof(ContributionType)`. If that fails, it frees `res` and returns NULL.  
  - It allocates an array `ContribRow` of `line_length` `ContributionType` elements. On failure, it frees `res` and returns NULL.  
  - It then loops over each of the `line_length` entries, allocating a `weights_size`‐byte array for the `.Weights` field of each `ContributionType`. On any failure in that loop, it frees all previously allocated weight arrays, the `ContribRow` array, and `res`, then returns NULL.  
  - If all allocations succeed, it returns the pointer to the fully initialized `LineContribType` structure.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

  - Integer‐overflow checks:  
    - The code invokes `overflow2(windows_size, sizeof(double))` and `overflow2(line_length, sizeof(ContributionType))` before doing each multiplication, preventing size arguments to `malloc` from wrapping around.  
  - Memory‐allocation failures:  
    - Every call to `gdMalloc` is checked. On allocation failure, the function cleans up any memory already allocated before returning NULL.  
  - Bounds and buffer safety:  
    - Memory is allocated exactly per the size checks; there are no raw pointer arithmetic or unbounded loops other than up to the validated `line_length`.  
  - No other resource or security‐critical operations (no string copies, no format strings, no use‐after‐free, no double frees, no uninitialized reads) are present.  

3. Decision

No, the code correctly checks for integer‐overflow, handles allocation failures at each step, and cleans up on error. It does not exhibit exploitable vulnerabilities.

1. Functional Analysis  
   - The function `skcipher_recvmsg` services a “receive” call on an AF_ALG socket set up for a block‐cipher (“skcipher”) operation.  
   - It grabs the kernel‐socket lock (`lock_sock`) to serialize access.  
   - It loops while there is space in the user’s scatter/gather iterator (`msg->msg_iter`):  
     • Retrieves the next incoming cipher‐text buffer from the per‐socket list (`ctx->tsgl`).  
     • Skips any zero‐length scatterlist entries.  
     • If no data is ready (`ctx->used == 0`), sleeps until new data arrives (`skcipher_wait_for_data`).  
     • Determines how many bytes to process: the lesser of available cipher‐text (`ctx->used`) and the user’s requested bytes.  
     • Builds an SG list for output into user space (`af_alg_make_sg`).  
     • If in “streaming” mode or if it won’t consume the entire input chunk, rounds the byte‐count down to a full cipher‐block multiple.  
     • If that leaves zero bytes to process, bails out with `-EINVAL`.  
     • Otherwise it programs the crypto API request (`ablkcipher_request_set_crypt`) and submits it for synchronous encryption or decryption.  
     • Frees the temporary SG list (`af_alg_free_sg`).  
     • On success, advances the internal SG list, the user’s iterator, and tallies bytes copied.  
   - When done, it wakes up any writers (`skcipher_wmem_wakeup`), releases the socket lock, and returns the number of bytes processed (or an error if nothing was copied).

2. Vulnerability Analysis  
   - **Bounds checking**: The code always clamps its processing size to `iov_iter_count(&msg->msg_iter)` and `ctx->used`, so it cannot overrun the user’s buffers or read past available cipher‐text.  
   - **Block alignment**: It rounds down to a full block size when streaming or partial chunk mode is in effect, ensuring the block cipher never sees partial blocks.  
   - **Null/empty lists**: The code assumes `ctx->tsgl` is nonempty when data is available; it explicitly waits (`skcipher_wait_for_data`) until data is enqueued.  
   - **Resource management**: Every temporary SG list is freed on both success and error paths. The socket lock is always released before return.  
   - **Error paths**: Negative error codes are returned only when no data has yet been copied; otherwise the function returns the actual byte count, preventing confusion of short reads with errors.  
   - **Concurrency**: Access is serialized by `lock_sock`/`release_sock`, and waiting for data uses the socket’s wait queue properly.  
   No buffer overflows, use-after-free, double free, race conditions, or alignment issues appear. The code follows the kernel’s AF_ALG synchronous block‐cipher pattern correctly.

3. Decision  
   No, the code contains no evident vulnerabilities. It enforces buffer bounds, proper block alignment, correct locking, and clean error handling.

crypto: fix af_alg_make_sg() conversion to iov_iter

Commit 1d10eb2f156f ("crypto: switch af_alg_make_sg() to iov_iter")
broke af_alg_make_sg() and skcipher_recvmsg() in the process of moving
them to the iov_iter interfaces.  The 'npages' calculation in the formar

1. Functional Analysis  

- The function nfc_llcp_set_remote_gb() is called with an NFC device pointer dev, a byte buffer gb, and its length gb_len.  
- It first checks that the provided gb_len is at least 3 bytes (enough to hold the “LLCP magic” header) and does not exceed NFC_MAX_GT_LEN. If the length is out of range, it returns –EINVAL.  
- It looks up the LLCP context (struct nfc_llcp_local) associated with the NFC device. If none is found, it logs an error and returns –ENODEV.  
- It zeroes out the entire local->remote_gb array (size NFC_MAX_GT_LEN), then copies exactly gb_len bytes from the caller’s gb buffer into local->remote_gb and records the length in local->remote_gb_len.  
- It compares the first three bytes of the newly stored remote_gb against a known llcp_magic sequence. If they don’t match, it logs “MAC does not support LLCP,” sets err to –EINVAL, and jumps to cleanup.  
- If the magic header is valid, it calls nfc_llcp_parse_gb_tlv(), passing in the TLV region starting at remote_gb[3] with length remote_gb_len–3.  
- In all cases it releases the local reference (nfc_llcp_local_put) and returns err (0 on success or a negative error code).  

2. Vulnerability Analysis  

- Buffer overflow: The code bounds-checks gb_len against NFC_MAX_GT_LEN before copying, and memcpy() is given exactly gb_len bytes into a buffer sized NFC_MAX_GT_LEN, so there is no overflow.  
- Underflow: Minimum length of 3 is enforced before any access to gb[0..2], so the memcmp() of the 3-byte header is safe.  
- Use-after-free/null-deref: The code checks that nfc_llcp_find_local() returns non-NULL before using local, and it always pairs the reference with a corresponding nfc_llcp_local_put() on exit.  
- Integer sign/size issues: gb_len is an unsigned 8-bit, compared as an integer to constants; no negative or wraparound scenarios occur.  
- TLV parsing: The slice &local->remote_gb[3] with length local->remote_gb_len–3 cannot exceed the original buffer bounds. Any deeper TLV parsing issues would reside in nfc_llcp_parse_gb_tlv(), not shown here.  

3. Decision  

No, the snippet contains no obvious vulnerabilities—it enforces length checks, avoids buffer overruns, and handles null contexts correctly.

In summary, this patch solves those use-after-free by

1. Re-implement the nfc_llcp_find_local(). The current version does not
grab the reference when getting the local from the linked list.  For
example, the llcp_sock_bind() gets the reference like below:

// llcp_sock_bind()

    local = nfc_llcp_find_local(dev); // A
    ..... \
           | raceable
    ..... /
    llcp_sock->local = nfc_llcp_local_get(local); // B

There is an apparent race window that one can  drop the reference
and free the local object fetched in (A) before (B) gets the reference.

2. Some callers of the nfc_llcp_find_local() do not grab the reference
at all. For example, the nfc_genl_llc_{{get/set}_params/sdreq} functions.
We add the nfc_llcp_local_put() for them. Moreover, we add the necessary
error handling function to put the reference.

3. Add the nfc_llcp_remove_local() helper. The local object is removed
from the linked list in local_release() when all reference is gone. This
patch removes it when nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called.

Therefore, every caller of nfc_llcp_find_local() will get a reference
even when the nfc_llcp_unregister_device() is called. This promises no
use-after-free for the local object is ever possible.

1. Functional Analysis

   Overall, this function implements an ioctl handler for a video-framebuffer device.  It examines the command (`cmd`) passed in and dispatches into one of three supported operations—or returns an error for any unsupported command.

   • FBIOGET_VBLANK  
     – Declares and zeroes a `struct fb_vblank`.  
     – Sets flags to indicate valid count, vcount, and vsync status.  
     – Reads a hardware register (`IVTV_REG_DEC_LINE_FIELD`), shifts it down, and normalizes line count by subtracting 312 or 262 depending on whether the card is running at 50 Hz or 60 Hz.  
     – If the (possibly wrapped) line number equals 1, marks that a vsync is in progress.  
     – Populates `.count`, `.vcount`, and `.hcount`, and copies the whole structure back to user space.  

   • FBIO_WAITFORVSYNC  
     – Prepares to sleep on `itv->vsync_waitq` in interruptible state.  
     – Calls `schedule_timeout()` for up to 50 ms (converted to jiffies).  
     – If the timeout elapses with no wakeup, returns `-ETIMEDOUT`; otherwise returns success.  
     – Cleans up the wait queue entry before returning.  

   • IVTVFB_IOC_DMA_FRAME  
     – Declares an `ivtvfb_dma_frame` structure in kernel space.  
     – Copies user-supplied arguments (source, destination offset, count) into it.  
     – Calls `ivtvfb_prep_frame()` to set up or queue the DMA transfer.  

   • default  
     – Prints a debug message about an unknown ioctl and returns `-EINVAL`.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   • Copying Data To/From User Space  
     – All user-space transfers use the standard `copy_from_user()`/`copy_to_user()` idioms, and errors are correctly turned into `-EFAULT`.  

   • Arithmetic / Underflow in Line-Count Normalization  
     – The code only subtracts 312 or 262 if the read line count is strictly greater than those values, avoiding any underflow or wrap here.  

   • Synchronization / Wait Queue  
     – The code sleeps interruptibly but does not explicitly handle signals by returning `-EINTR`. A signal that fires inside `schedule_timeout()` will cause it to wake early and return a nonzero remaining jiffies, making the ioctl return success even though no vsync occurred. This is a minor logic issue (spuriously successful wakeup) rather than a security flaw.  

   • Input Validation for DMA Arguments  
     – `ivtvfb_io­ctl()` itself does not validate the numerical fields inside the copied-in `ivtvfbfb_dma_frame` struct (e.g. `dest_offset` or `count` may be out of expected bounds). It relies entirely on `ivtvfb_prep_frame()` to perform any necessary range checks before programming DMA hardware. If that downstream function does not properly clamp or reject out-of-range values, a malicious user could potentially provoke an out-of-bounds DMA, leading to memory corruption.  

3. Decision

No, the shown code snippet itself does not contain any direct buffer overflows or user-memory dereferences without proper checks. It correctly uses the kernel’s copy_to/from_user mechanisms and guards the arithmetic. The only area that could become a security problem is insufficient validation of `ivtvfb_dma_frame` fields—however, that risk must be ruled out by inspecting `ivtvfb_prep_frame()`.

original_information.Summary: Race condition in the audit_log_single_execve_arg function in kernel/auditsc.c in the Linux kernel through 4.7 allows local users to bypass intended character-set restrictions or disrupt system-call auditing by changing a certain string, aka a *double fetch* vulnerability.
original_information.commit_message:
audit: fix a double fetch in audit_log_single_execve_arg()

There is a double fetch problem in audit_log_single_execve_arg()
where we first check the execve(2) argumnets for any "bad" characters
which would require hex encoding and then re-fetch the arguments for
logging in the audit record[1].  Of course this leaves a window of
opportunity for an unsavory application to munge with the data.

This patch reworks things by only fetching the argument data once[2]
into a buffer where it is scanned and logged into the audit
records(s).  In addition to fixing the double fetch, this patch
improves on the original code in a few other ways: better handling
of large arguments which require encoding, stricter record length
checking, and some performance improvements (completely unverified,
but we got rid of some strlen() calls, that's got to be a good
thing).

As part of the development of this patch, I've also created a basic
regression test for the audit-testsuite, the test can be tracked on
GitHub at the following link:

 * https://github.com/linux-audit/audit-testsuite/issues/25

[1] If you pay careful attention, there is actually a triple fetch
problem due to a strnlen_user() call at the top of the function.

[2] This is a tiny white lie, we do make a call to strnlen_user()
prior to fetching the argument data.  I don't like it, but due to the
way the audit record is structured we really have no choice unless we
copy the entire argument at once (which would require a rather
wasteful allocation).  The good news is that with this patch the
kernel no longer relies on this strnlen_user() value for anything
beyond recording it in the log, we also update it with a trustworthy
value whenever possible.

Reported-by: Pengfei Wang <wpengfeinudt@gmail.com>
Cc: <stable@vger.kernel.org>

6. It constructs the full socket pathname in `name` by reserving enough space for `dir + "/" + SOCK_FILENAME + uname`, then appending those components in order.
7. It frees the temporary C‐string `dir` and logs the target socket path.
8. It zeros a `sockaddr_un local` struct, sets `sun_family = AF_UNIX`, and uses `strncpy` to copy `name.c_str()` into `local.sun_path`, preventing overflow by limiting to `sizeof(local.sun_path)-1`.
9. It calls `connect(s, (struct sockaddr *)&local, sizeof local)`. On failure it closes the socket, logs a non‐fatal “connect” error if this is a retry, and returns –1.
10. After a successful connect, it calls `getpeereid(s, &seuid, &segid)` to fetch the peer’s effective UID/GID. If the peer’s UID doesn’t match `geteuid()`, it treats it as a credential mismatch, logs a debug message, closes the socket, and returns –1.

• Buffer overflow in `local.sun_path`:  
  The code zeroes the entire struct, then uses `strncpy(..., sizeof-1)`, ensuring no overflow and a NUL terminator (because of the initial zero‐fill). Safe.  

• Pathmanipulation / symlink attack:  
  The directory is either from a wide‐string `wdir` or `"/tmp"`, and the final socket filename is predictable (`/tmp/…SOCK_FILENAME…username`). However fishd’s own socket creation and credential check (`getpeereid`) ensure that only processes with the same effective UID can fully connect—so no privilege escalation occurs.  

• Use of full `sizeof local` in `connect`:

• Not checking `wcs2str` or `wcs2string` return values:  
  In theory these could fail (return null), but typical implementations either throw or exit, and the code does not dereference a null pointer here. It might be prudent to check, but this is a minor robustness issue, not a security flaw.  

Overall there is no unhandled memory corruption, no race condition leading to privilege escalation, and the peer credential check prevents connecting to a malicious socket owned by another user.

No, the code does not contain exploitable vulnerabilities. It correctly bounds buffers, authenticates the peer, and handles errors.

   - The function jiffies_to_timespec takes an input “jiffies” count (an unsigned long) and a pointer to a struct timespec.
   - It wants to convert the number of jiffies into a standard seconds/nanoseconds timespec representation.
   - First, it computes (u64)jiffies * TICK_NSEC, where TICK_NSEC is the number of nanoseconds per jiffy; casting to u64 ensures the intermediate product uses 64-bit precision.
   - It then calls div_u64_rem(…, NSEC_PER_SEC, &rem), which divides the 64-bit nanoseconds value by one billion (the number of nanoseconds per second).  
     – The quotient becomes tv_sec (whole seconds).  
     – The remainder (modulo one second) is stored in rem.
   - Finally, tv_nsec is set to rem, yielding a full seconds+nanoseconds conversion.

     • The multiplication is done in 64 bits. On common architectures, unsigned long jiffies is at most 32 bits (so jiffies ≤ ~4×10^9), and TICK_NSEC ≤ 10^9, giving a product ≤ ~4×10^18, well under 2^64.

     → No practical overflow risk.
   - Divide-by-zero:  
     • NSEC_PER_SEC is a constant (1,000,000,000), never zero.  
     → Safe.
   - Pointer safety:  
     • The caller must pass a valid struct timespec pointer. This is a normal kernel-API precondition.  
     → No evidence of buffer overrun or invalid write aside from the usual requirement of a valid pointer.
   - Other issues:  
     • No user-supplied length fields or unchecked memory accesses.  
     • No syscall boundary or untrusted input parsing here.  
     → No exploitable memory or logic flaw.

3. Decision

   No, this code does not contain a vulnerability. It correctly performs a jiffies-to-timespec conversion using safe 64-bit arithmetic and a single division.

x86 is the only arch right now, which provides an optimized for

original_information.commit_message:
Fix SPNEGO context aliasing bugs [CVE-2015-2695]

The SPNEGO mechanism currently replaces its context handle with the
mechanism context handle upon establishment, under the assumption that
most GSS functions are only called after context establishment.  This
assumption is incorrect, and can lead to aliasing violations for some
programs.  Maintain the SPNEGO context structure after context
establishment and refer to it in all GSS methods.  Add initiate and
opened flags to the SPNEGO context structure for use in
gss_inquire_context() prior to context establishment.

CVE-2015-2695:

In MIT krb5 1.5 and later, applications which call
gss_inquire_context() on a partially-established SPNEGO context can
cause the GSS-API library to read from a pointer using the wrong type,
generally causing a process crash.  This bug may go unnoticed, because
the most common SPNEGO authentication scenario establishes the context
after just one call to gss_accept_sec_context().  Java server
applications using the native JGSS provider are vulnerable to this
bug.  A carefully crafted SPNEGO packet might allow the
gss_inquire_context() call to succeed with attacker-determined
results, but applications should not make access control decisions
based on gss_inquire_context() results prior to context establishment.

- The function ReadPCDImage opens a blob (file or memory) for reading a Kodak Photo CD (PCD) image, using the supplied ImageInfo and ExceptionInfo.
- It allocates a 6144-byte header buffer and reads 3×0x800 bytes from the blob.  It checks for the “PCD” or “PCD_OPA” signature and extracts a rotation flag and the number of embedded images.
- Based on either the user’s requested scene or the file’s built-in overview‐levels, it computes the pixel dimensions (width, height) for the desired resolution (ranging from 192×128 up to 6144×4096).
- It sets up the Image structure (columns, rows, depth) and calls SetImageExtent to reserve pixel storage in ImageMagick’s internal format.
- It allocates three scratch buffers (luma, chroma1, chroma2) large enough to hold all the Y/Cb/Cr data at the computed resolution.
- It seeks past the photographic data offset (1–93 blocks of 0x800 bytes, depending on scene and overview).
- If the file is an overview (thumbnail) file, it loops over each embedded image, reads interleaved Y/Cb/Cr planes, calls Upsample to expand the Cb/Cr planes, then for each scanline queues a pixel row, writes R=Y, G=Cb, B=Cr (using ScaleCharToQuantum), sets the colorspace to YCC (or sRGB if PCDS), and chains images as needed.
- If it is not an overview, it reads the interleaved Y/Cb/Cr planes for the single requested image, possibly does a multi‐stage delta decode for large resolutions (1024, 2048, even 4096 rows), upsamples the chroma planes, then writes out the pixels just as above.
- After reading all data, it frees the scratch buffers, checks for unexpected EOF, closes the blob, optionally rotates the image by ±90° if the header demanded it, sets fixed CCIR-709/D65 chromaticities and a 1/2.2 gamma, converts to sRGB if needed, and returns the head of the image list.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Memory allocation: sizes for the header (3×0x800 bytes) and the luma/chroma buffers are based on the computed width/height (capped by scene ≤ 6, i.e. ≤ 6144×4096).  Allocations use AcquireQuantumMemory, which checks for integer overflow of “count × quantum” and returns NULL on overflow or OOM.  All allocations are checked for NULL, and on failure they free any prior buffers and throw a ResourceLimitError.
- Buffer reads/writes: all ReadBlob calls are bounded by the known plane sizes (width or width/2).  Upsample writes to the same size buffers.  Writing to the Image pixels uses QueueAuthenticPixels/SyncAuthenticPixels, which verify the extent and forbid overruns.
- Header parsing: the code reads exactly 6144 bytes, checks the signature before indexing header[0x0e02] or header[10..11], and then immediately frees the buffer, so there is no out-of-bounds or use-after-free access.
- Loop counts: scene is clamped to 1..6 (and forced to 1 for overviews) so loops over y, x, j (number_images up to 65535) cannot exceed predictable bounds.  The worst‐case allocation is large but fails cleanly if the system cannot satisfy it.
- Error handling: all filesystem/IO errors, unexpected EOF, allocation failures, and invalid headers trigger proper exceptions and cleanup.  There is no unchecked pointer arithmetic or unbounded memcpy/memmove.
- Denial-of-service: a malicious header could advertise 65535 embedded images, forcing repeated large allocations and decode loops, but the code will quickly hit memory limits or slow I/O—this is a resource exhaustion, not a memory corruption vulnerability.

3. Decision

No, the code applies appropriate bounds checks, overflow‐safe allocation, and robust error handling, and contains no evident buffer-overflow, integer-overflow, or use-after-free vulnerabilities.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `canonify_unencrypted_header` takes three parameters:
  • `buff`     – a pre-allocated output buffer  
  • `offset`   – a pointer to the current write position within `buff`  
  • `buffsize` – the total size of `buff`  

- Internally there is a table `canonifyTable[]` of `TOP_ELEMENT_CONTROL` entries.  Each entry carries:  
  • `element`   – a pointer (by address) to a data payload (or NULL)  
  • `length`    – the current payload length  
  • `allocated` – the total allocated size for that payload  
  • Flags:  
    – `required` (payload must be present)  
    – `addtag`   (re-insert a tag+BER-length header)  
    – `truncate` (produce a shorter “canonical” form)  
  • `tag`       – the one-byte identifier to insert if `addtag` is true  

- The function loops over that table until `t->element` is NULL.  For each entry:  
  a) It reads the current `len` and `allocated`.  
  b) If the field is `required` but the element pointer is NULL, it bails out with FALSE.  
  c) If the element pointer is non-NULL:  
     1. If `addtag` is set, it writes one tag byte at `buff[offset]`, increments `*offset`, then calls `encode_ber_len()` to write the BER length of the payload and advances `*offset` by however many bytes that encoding took.  
     2. If `truncate` is set, it replaces `len` with a small constant (3 + 2×sizeOfBER(len)).  
     3. It checks whether there is still room in `buff` for `len` more bytes (`buffsize < *offset + len ? FALSE : ok`) and whether the source payload was at least `len` bytes (`allocated < len ? FALSE : ok`).  
     4. It copies `len` bytes from the external payload into `buff + *offset`, then advances `*offset` by `len`.  
     5. If `addtag` was set, it nulls out the original `t->element` pointer (to avoid re-inserting).  

- If it finishes the table without errors, it returns TRUE.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Bounds checks on the bulk `memcpy()`:  
  • It verifies `buffsize >= *offset + len` before the copy, so in normal unsigned arithmetic it prevents writing past the end of `buff`.  
  • It also checks `allocated >= len` so it cannot read past the source buffer.

- Small gaps in checking header bytes:  
  • The code writes the one-byte `tag` and then calls `encode_ber_len()` before doing *any* bounds check for those header bytes.  If `buffsize` were smaller than `*offset + 1` (or smaller than `*offset + encode_ber_len(…)`), those initial writes could overflow the buffer.  In practice the calling code must guarantee that `buffsize` is large enough for all tags+lengths plus the data, so this is an assumption rather than a direct bug—but it is an unchecked write.

- Integer-overflow corner case:  
  • The check `buffsize < *offset + len` uses unsigned 32-bit math.  If `*offset + len` wraps around past 2^32, the comparison may be bypassed and then `memcpy()` can also write out of bounds.  In realistic use the function keeps `*offset` ≤ `buffsize` and `buffsize` is far below 2^32, so the wrap-around never happens—but the arithmetic is not hardened against a maliciously large `offset` or `len` field.

Overall, the code *intends* to prevent overreads and overwrites and does so for the main payload copy, but it makes two un-checked assumptions:
  1) there is always room for the tag+BER-length bytes,  
  2) no 32-bit wrap-around of `*offset + len` occurs.

3. Decision

No, the code does not contain an actual vulnerability *provided* that the caller has correctly initialized `offset = 0` (or another small value) and passed a `buffsize` large enough to hold every header tag+length and payload.  The only risks are:
  - un-checked writes of 1–4 header bytes if `buffsize` is too small,  
  - potential 32-bit overflow if someone allowed `*offset` + `len` to wrap.

But in normal usage (small, sequential offsets and properly pre-sized buffers) those conditions do not arise, so there is no exploitable flaw here.

The function tt_face_load_font_dir loads the SFNT (TrueType/OpenType) table directory into a TT_Face object. In broad strokes:

 a) It records the current stream position (sfnt.offset) and reads the SFNT “offset table”:
    - format_tag (4-byte signature)  
    - num_tables (number of table records)  
    - search_range, entry_selector, range_shift  

 b) If the font is not CFF-flavored (OTTO), it calls check_table_dir to do a preliminary validation of the directory structure.

 c) It stores num_tables and format_tag in the face object and allocates an array face->dir_tables with one TT_TableRec per table.

 d) It seeks to the start of the table records (offset + 12 bytes) and enters a frame large enough to hold all table records (num_tables × 16 bytes each).  

 e) It loops over each table record, reading:
    - Tag (4-byte identifier)  
    - CheckSum (32-bit)  
    - Offset (32-bit file offset)  
    - Length (32-bit size)  

 f) For each record it rejects entries whose Offset/Length would extend past the end of the font file. Valid records are kept in the dir_tables array (invalid ones are skipped).  

 g) It exits the frame and returns FT_Error (0 on success or an appropriate error code).

 • Integer or buffer overflows when multiplying num_tables×16?  
   - num_tables is read from the file header; in practice it’s small.  
   - FT_QNEW_ARRAY and FT_FRAME_ENTER internally check for excessive sizes or overflow, returning an error rather than overrunning memory.

   - The code checks `entry->Length > stream->size` and `entry->Offset > stream->size - entry->Length` before accepting an entry, ensuring no read beyond the stream.

 • Maliciously large num_tables leading to huge allocations or denial-of-service?  
   - FT_QNEW_ARRAY will fail if the requested size is unreasonably large.  
   - FT_FRAME_ENTER (and the underlying stream API) also refuses to map more bytes than are available.

All boundary checks and API-level safeguards prevent reading or writing past allocated buffers. No unchecked arithmetic leads to exploitable overflows or out-of-bounds memory access.

No, the code does not contain exploitable vulnerabilities. It correctly bounds-checks file offsets, lengths, and array sizes.

original_information.commit_msg:
Excessive allocation of memory in dtls1_preprocess_fragment()

This issue is very similar to CVE-2016-6307 described in the previous
commit. The underlying defect is different but the security analysis and
impacts are the same except that it impacts DTLS.

A DTLS message includes 3 bytes for its length in the header for the
message.
This would allow for messages up to 16Mb in length. Messages of this length
are excessive and OpenSSL includes a check to ensure that a peer is sending
reasonably sized messages in order to avoid too much memory being consumed
to service a connection. A flaw in the logic of version 1.1.0 means that
memory for the message is allocated too early, prior to the excessive
message length check. Due to way memory is allocated in OpenSSL this could
mean an attacker could force up to 21Mb to be allocated to service a
connection. This could lead to a Denial of Service through memory
exhaustion. However, the excessive message length check still takes place,
and this would cause the connection to immediately fail. Assuming that the
application calls SSL_free() on the failed conneciton in a timely manner
then the 21Mb of allocated memory will then be immediately freed again.
Therefore the excessive memory allocation will be transitory in nature.
This then means that there is only a security impact if:

1) The application does not call SSL_free() in a timely manner in the
event that the connection fails
or
2) The application is working in a constrained environment where there
is very little free memory
or
3) The attacker initiates multiple connection attempts such that there
are multiple connections in a state where memory has been allocated for
the connection; SSL_free() has not yet been called; and there is
insufficient memory to service the multiple requests.

Except in the instance of (1) above any Denial Of Service is likely to
be transitory because as soon as the connection fails the memory is
subsequently freed again in the SSL_free() call. However there is an
increased risk during this period of application crashes due to the lack
of memory - which would then mean a more serious Denial of Service.

This issue does not affect TLS users.

Issue was reported by Shi Lei (Gear Team, Qihoo 360 Inc.).

   The function `call_backend()` serves as a wrapper to invoke a CUPS backend program based on a device URI. In detail:

   • Parse the scheme  
     – Copy the input URI into a local buffer `scheme`.  
     – Truncate at the first colon (`:`) to isolate the scheme (e.g. “socket”, “ipp”).  
     – Validate that the scheme does not contain a slash or equal “.”/“..”.  
     – On failure, print an error and exit with `CUPS_BACKEND_FAILED`.  

   • Determine backend directory  
     – Read the environment variable `CUPS_SERVERBIN`; fall back to the compile-time `CUPS_SERVERBIN` if unset.  

   • Disallow direct file output  
     – If the URI begins “file:” or with a slash, reject it.  

   • Build arguments for the real backend  
     – Fill `backend_argv` with the original URI and the six standard CUPS backend arguments (`job-id`, `user`, `job-name`, `copies`, `options`, `file`).  
     – Assemble `backend_path` as “<CUPS_SERVERBIN>/backend/<scheme>” using `snprintf`.  

   • Set environment and debug print  
     – Export `DEVICE_URI=<uri>`.  
     – Print debug messages showing the exact exec call.  

   • Fork and exec the backend  
     – In the child: call `execv(backend_path, backend_argv)`. On error, print `strerror(errno)` and exit.  
     – In the parent: wait for the child, interpret its exit status or terminating signal, and return that as the function’s result.  

2. Vulnerability Analysis

   • Buffer overflows  
     – `strncat(scheme, uri, sizeof(scheme)-1)` and `snprintf(backend_path, sizeof(backend_path), ...)` both cap their writes and check the return lengths. No overflow is possible here.  

   • Command injection  
     – The code uses `execv()` directly without invoking a shell, and builds the argv array explicitly from parameters. No untrusted data is passed to a shell interpreter.  

   • Path traversal or arbitrary backend execution  
     – The scheme is forbidden to contain ‘/’, ‘.’, or ‘..’, so an attacker cannot directly traverse directories within the backend path.  
     – The only tunable part of the backend path is the environment variable `CUPS_SERVERBIN`. If an administrator unwisely sets `CUPS_SERVERBIN` to an attacker-controlled directory, a malicious backend binary could be placed there. But this is an administrative configuration issue, not a flaw in the code itself.  

   • Unchecked environment calls  
     – `setenv()` return value is ignored, but failure is unlikely in normal operation (and would normally only occur in very low-memory situations).  

   • Debug logging  
     – All user strings are printed with `%s`, so there is no format-string vulnerability.  

   Overall, the code performs adequate input validation on the URI scheme, uses safe string functions, avoids the shell, and reasonably constructs and executes the backend. No exploitable vulnerabilities are evident in isolation.  

3. Decision

   No, the code does not contain vulnerabilities.

1. Functional Analysis

- The function `snd_ctl_elem_read` handles a user request to read a mixer/control element value from an ALSA sound card.
- It takes two inputs:
  • `card` – the sound card context  
  • `control` – a pre-populated structure identifying which control element and space for the returned value  
- It acquires a read lock (`down_read(&card->controls_rwsem)`) to protect the control list against concurrent modifications.
- It looks up the control by its identifier (`snd_ctl_find_id`), and returns `-ENOENT` if not found.
- It computes an index offset if the control has multiple elements, then picks the relevant volatile control data (`vd`).
- It checks if the control permits reads (`vd->access & SNDRV_CTL_ELEM_ACCESS_READ`) and has a `get` callback; otherwise returns `-EPERM`.
- It reconstructs the full ID in `control->id` (for multi-element controls) via `snd_ctl_build_ioff`.
- If debug mode is enabled (`CONFIG_SND_CTL_DEBUG`), it builds an `info` struct and calls `__snd_ctl_elem_info` purely to validate the request format.
- Unless validation is disabled, it calls `fill_remaining_elem_value` to pre-fill the output buffer with a known pattern (`0xdeadbeef`) to spot any uninitialized fields.
- It powers up (or ensures the device is awake) via `snd_power_ref_and_wait`, then invokes the control’s `get` callback to actually copy the hardware value into the user’s buffer.
- It drops the power reference (`snd_power_unref`) and checks for any overflow or out-of-bounds writes by comparing what was returned against the earlier pattern (`sanity_check_elem_value`).
- On any error, it jumps to the `unlock` label, releases the read lock, and propagates the error code. On success, it releases the lock and returns zero.

2. Vulnerability Analysis

- Race conditions on the control list are prevented by holding `controls_rwsem` in read mode throughout the lookup and execution of `get`. Concurrent writers would block until the read lock is released.
- Only controls that explicitly allow reads and supply a valid `get` callback are executed, preventing accidental or unauthorized memory access.
- The code pre-fills the entire output buffer with a sentinel pattern and then verifies afterwards, catching any under- or over-writes by a buggy `get` method.
- Error paths all route through the `unlock` label, ensuring the semaphore is always released and there are no lock-leak scenarios.
- Power management reference counting is balanced: on every successful or failed `snd_power_ref_and_wait` there is a matching `snd_power_unref`, avoiding hangs or runaway references.
- No unbounded copies of user-provided data occur; all array accesses (control ID arrays, vd array) are indexed after bounds checks in helper routines like `snd_ctl_find_id` and `snd_ctl_get_ioff`.
- The only potential concern would be a buggy or malicious `get` implementation of a custom control, but the pre-/post-pattern validation would detect overruns and return `-EINVAL` rather than crash or leak data.

3. Decision

No, this code does not contain any obvious vulnerabilities. It employs proper locking, access checks, buffer initialization, and post-validation to prevent common read-side flaws.
